| | **South Coast Rail** is a project to expand the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system into the [South Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_/(Massachusetts/) "South Coast (Massachusetts)") region of [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), United States. The first phase opened on March 24, 2025, becoming part of the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line"). It extended service from [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts") via [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") with branches to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). Six stations and two layover yards were constructed and 36.1 miles (58.1 km) of freight railroad track were rebuilt for passenger service. Previous passenger service to the South Coast ran over four different routes: via [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts"), via [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Massachusetts "Randolph, Massachusetts"), and via Middleborough. The first lines reached Taunton in 1836, New Bedford in 1840, and Fall River in 1846. The network of lines in southeastern Massachusetts was consolidated by 1888 under the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad"), which was in turn acquired by the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893. Passenger service peaked in the early 20th century and declined thereafter, with the final service to the South Coast in 1958. The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) began planning the restoration of South Coast service in the 1980s. Feasibility studies were released in 1990 and 1995; the MBTA filed plans for a route using a new bypass near [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro,_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts") in 1995. Environmental impact statements instead recommended a route via Stoughton, which required reactivating an abandoned section of rail line. Planning was suspended in 2002 due to increasing costs but resumed several years later. In 2010, the state purchased the rail lines from [CSX Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation"). Environmental impact statements in 2011 and 2013 again recommended the Stoughton route; state officials mandated that the service be electrified. In March 2017, the project was split into two phases due to high costs and long construction timelines. Phase 1 would provide interim diesel service to Fall River and New Bedford via Middleborough as an extension of the existing [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line"). Phase 2 would complete the northern section of the project between Stoughton and Taunton and add electrification to the Phase 1 portion. Phase 1 construction began in 2019 with a projected cost of $1.047 billion and opened on March 24, 2025. Phase 2, which is not funded, would result in a total projected cost of $3.42 billion if built. [![Image 125: A high-level railway station platform with trains on both sides](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ae/Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg/250px-Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg) Two trains at [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station") The project, primarily located in the [South Coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_/(Massachusetts/) "South Coast (Massachusetts)") region of Massachusetts, is split into two phases. Phase 1 opened on March 24, 2025, as part of the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line "Fall River/New Bedford Line"). It was an extension of the existing [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") using diesel-hauled trains. The Phase 1 routing splits from the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line") in downtown [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts"), with [Middleborough station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station") replacing [Middleborough/Lakeville station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station "Middleborough/Lakeville station"). It runs west along the [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary") through [Lakeville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakeville,_Massachusetts "Lakeville, Massachusetts") and [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") to Cotley Junction, where it turns southeast onto the [New Bedford Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Secondary "New Bedford Secondary") and reaches [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station"). At [Myricks Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") in [Berkley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berkley,_Massachusetts "Berkley, Massachusetts") it splits into two southern branches. The Fall River Branch follows the [Fall River Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Secondary "Fall River Secondary") southwest through [Freetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown,_Massachusetts "Freetown, Massachusetts") and [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts"), with stops at [Freetown station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown_station "Freetown station") and [Fall River station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_station "Fall River station"). The New Bedford Branch follows the New Bedford Main Line southeast through Lakeville, Freetown, and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"), with stops at [Church Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Church_Street_station_/(MBTA/) "Church Street station (MBTA)") and [New Bedford station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_station "New Bedford station").[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-2)[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 48 Phase 1 added passenger service to 36.1 miles (58.1 km) of track. The 7.1-mile (11.4 km) section of the Middleboro Secondary used for the project is single track with one siding. The 4.3 miles (6.9 km) of the New Bedford Main Line between Cotley Junction and Myricks Junction are double track, while the 14.0 miles (22.5 km) between Myricks Junction and New Bedford are a mix of single and double track. The 10.7 miles (17.2 km) of the Fall River Secondary are also a mixture.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 52  [Positive train control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Positive_train_control "Positive train control") was installed on the lines for the project.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 54  Except for sidings and the Church Street–New Bedford section, the track was built to support passenger train speeds of 79 miles per hour (127 km/h).[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 53  [Layover yards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority_yards "List of Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority yards") were built at Weaver's Cove in northern Fall River and Wamsutta near the New Bedford station.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 4  The six new stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 56–58  Construction cost for Phase 1 was estimated as $1.047 billion in 2019 (equivalent to $1.26 billion in 2024).[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-spring2019-3) [![Image 126: A one-story Richardsonian Romanesque train station next to a disused track](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/ba/North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest%2C_June_2017.JPG/250px-North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest%2C_June_2017.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:North_Easton_station_from_the_southwest,_June_2017.JPG) The former station building at North Easton, proposed to be the site of Easton Village station Phase 2 ("full build"), which is proposed but not funded, would turn the South Coast lines into an extension of the Stoughton Branch of the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line"). From [Stoughton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station"), it would run south along the former [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") through [Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton,_Massachusetts "Easton, Massachusetts"), [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts"), and Taunton. At Weir Junction in Taunton, it would turn southeast onto the New Bedford Main Line, meeting the Phase 1 routing at Cotley Junction. New intermediate stops would be added at North Easton station, [Easton Village station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton_Village_station "Easton Village station"), [Raynham Place station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham_Place_station "Raynham Place station"), and [Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)"). The Fall River Branch would also be extended south to a new [Battleship Cove station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship_Cove_station "Battleship Cove station"). The Stoughton Branch, the new segments, and the Phase 1 segments (except for the Middleboro Secondary) would be electrified.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-4) Total cost for the both phases was estimated as $3.4 billion in 2017 (equivalent to $4.1 billion in 2024).[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5) Unlike Phase 1, Phase 2 would involve reactivation of [previously abandoned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abandoned_railway#In_the_United_States "Abandoned railway") railroad right-of-way, as the portion between southern Stoughton and eastern Taunton was abandoned around the 1960s.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-fseir-6): 1–6 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-abandoned-7) In southern Easton and northern Raynham, the route passes through the [Hockomock Swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hockomock_Swamp "Hockomock Swamp") on a low embankment, which is partially rewilded though used by pedestrians and [all-terrain vehicle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-terrain_vehicle "All-terrain vehicle") riders. The swamp is a designated [Area of Critical Environmental Concern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Area_of_Critical_Environmental_Concern_/(Massachusetts/) "Area of Critical Environmental Concern (Massachusetts)") and houses several endangered species including the [blue-spotted salamander](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue-spotted_salamander "Blue-spotted salamander").[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-8)[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-app417a-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-10) An 8,500-foot (2,600 m) trestle atop the embankment is proposed to allow animals to pass under the tracks and limit the disturbance to the existing ground. The trestle would use concrete box girders on piles spaced at 50 feet (15 m), with a maintenance siding in the middle.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-app32c-11)[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-13) [![Image 127: A postcard of a railway station with an Egyptian Revival style facade](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/90/New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg/250px-New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:New_Bedford_old_station_postcard.jpg) The first station in New Bedford Previous passenger service to the South Coast ran over four different routes: via [Mansfield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansfield,_Massachusetts "Mansfield, Massachusetts"), via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts"), via [Randolph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph,_Massachusetts "Randolph, Massachusetts"), and via [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough,_Massachusetts "Middleborough, Massachusetts"). The first rail line to reach the area was the [Taunton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_Branch_Railroad "Taunton Branch Railroad"), which connected with the [Boston and Providence Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_and_Providence_Railroad "Boston and Providence Railroad") (B&P) at Mansfield. It opened to [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts") in August 1836; a closely affiliated extension, the [New Bedford and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_and_Taunton_Railroad "New Bedford and Taunton Railroad"), opened to New Bedford in July 1840.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 39–398  The [Middleborough and Taunton Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_and_Taunton_Railroad "Middleborough and Taunton Railroad") opened in July 1856; it connected with the New Bedford and Taunton at Cotley Junction south of Taunton.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 398 The first segment of what would become the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)") opened from [Myricks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Myricks,_Massachusetts "Myricks, Massachusetts") (on the New Bedford and Taunton) to Fall River on June 9, 1845.[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1911report-15)[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-16) The rest of the line opened in 1846 from Myricks through Middleborough to [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/)#History "Braintree station (MBTA)") on the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), creating a second route from Fall River to Boston. The next year, owner [Richard Borden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Borden "Richard Borden") founded the [Fall River Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Line "Fall River Line"), which operated New York–Fall River steamship service. It connected with the "Boat Train" on the Fall River Railroad to provide New York–Boston through service.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 403  The Old Colony Railroad and the Fall River Railroad merged in 1854 as the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). It merged with the [Newport and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Newport and Fall River Railroad") in 1863 to become the [Old Colony and Newport Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Newport_Railway "Old Colony and Newport Railway"), then with the [Cape Cod Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Railroad "Cape Cod Railroad") in 1872 to become the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad").[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 The [Stoughton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch_Railroad "Stoughton Branch Railroad") opened in April 1845 from Stoughton to [Canton Junction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canton_Junction_station "Canton Junction station") on the B&P.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 181  An extension, the [Easton Branch Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Easton_Branch_Railroad&action=edit&redlink=1 "Easton Branch Railroad (page does not exist)"), opened to [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton,_Massachusetts "North Easton, Massachusetts") on May 16, 1855.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 29  In 1863, the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") began construction on a line between Somerset Junction (north of Fall River) and [Braintree Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree,_Massachusetts "Braintree, Massachusetts") – both on the Old Colony and Newport – via Taunton, North Easton, and Randolph. The Old Colony and Newport purchased the potential competitor in 1865 and opened it on September 24, 1866.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-secondsection-18): 11 [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 393  It used the Easton Branch Railroad between North Easton and Stoughton Junction (south of Stoughton); passenger service ended between Stoughton and Stoughton Junction. The new route via Randolph was shorter than the Middleborough and Mansfield routes; it became the Old Colony's primary Fall River–Boston routing.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394 [![Image 128: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b6/OC1893.jpg/250px-OC1893.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:OC1893.jpg) [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") network in 1893 The Taunton Branch Railroad opened a branch from Attleboro Junction (west of Taunton) to [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro,_Massachusetts "Attleboro, Massachusetts") in 1871. The company merged with the New Bedford and Taunton in 1874 as the [New Bedford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford_Railroad "New Bedford Railroad").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 398  The Old Colony acquired the Middleborough and Taunton Railroad in 1874 and a successor of the New Bedford Railroad in 1879.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 399  Around 1882, the Old Colony opened the [Whittenton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittenton_Branch "Whittenton Branch") between Whittenton Junction (near Attleboro Junction) and [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts"). It allowed trains on the Dighton and Somerset to serve [Taunton Central station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Amtrak/) "Taunton station (Amtrak)") rather than [Dean Street station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)"), thus consolidating Taunton's passenger services at a single station.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394 The Old Colony acquired the B&P in 1888, consolidating all the railways in southeastern Massachusetts under a single owner. The company expanded Mansfield–New Bedford service and routed some Fall River and New Bedford trains via Stoughton at times.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 31  The [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") (New Haven) leased the Old Colony in 1893.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 379  By 1898, daily South Coast service via Mansfield included six Taunton–Boston round trips and one New Bedford–Boston round trip plus nine New Bedford–Mansfield round trips that connected with Boston trains at Mansfield. Service via Randolph included one Taunton–Boston round trip and four [Newport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newport,_Rhode_Island "Newport, Rhode Island")–Fall River–Boston round trips. There were three Fall River–Boston round trips via Middleborough.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34 The opening of [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station") in 1898 allowed increases in through service; by 1906; eleven of the fourteen daily New Bedford–Mansfield round trips ran to and from Boston.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Service timed for Boston commuting had been available from Taunton and New Bedford via Mansfield since around 1885.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 31  Fall River never had a strong commuter market to Boston; commuter service via Middleborough was available for several years starting in 1915.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 [\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-secondsection-18): 30  Commuter service via Randolph never ran further south than North Easton.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 95 Cutbacks to service began during World War I and continued thereafter. Service between Mansfield and New Bedford was reduced sharply to five daily round trips, and Fall River service via Middleborough dwindled.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34 [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 403  The New Haven resumed running South Coast trains via Stoughton during and after the war.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Use of the Randolph route ended around 1924.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 394  By 1927, all service to New Bedford and Fall River ran via Stoughton, save for a single Fall River round trip that ran via Middleborough until 1931.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34, 96  Service on the southern part of the Dighton and Somerset ended in 1932, with Fall River service routed via Myricks thereafter.[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 395 South Coast service was rerouted via Mansfield in 1937 during the early stages of the [88 stations case](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/88_stations_case "88 stations case"), which also brought the end of service south of Fall River in 1938.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 34  Fall River service was reduced to Taunton shuttles during World War II. New Bedford service was reduced to three round trips in March 1949, and the Fall River shuttles were discontinued that September. Most New Bedford service was routed via Stoughton in 1950; both routes were used for several years.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 35  Fall River shuttles resumed in June 1952.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-19)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 35 All service was routed via Stoughton in 1955 when a grade separation project at Mansfield cut the branch line. By that time there were three New Bedford–Boston round trips – one with a Fall River shuttle – and one Fall River–Boston trip.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 36  That remaining service ended on September 5, 1958, as the New Haven cut its unprofitable Old Colony Division; the remaining passenger service on the division ended the next year.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 36, 96  Freight service to the South Coast continued, though the remainder of the Dighton and Somerset was abandoned in the 1960s and 1970s.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-abandoned-7) The New Haven merged in late 1968 into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central"), which merged into [Conrail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conrail "Conrail") in 1976. Passenger service continued on the ex-B&P, including the Stoughton Branch, eventually becoming the [Providence/Stoughton Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Providence/Stoughton_Line "Providence/Stoughton Line").[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sne-14): 19 South Coast Rail planning ------------------------- \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=8 "Edit section: South Coast Rail planning")\] ### Restoration planning (1980s–2003) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=9 "Edit section: Restoration planning (1980s–2003)")\] The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in 1964 to subsidize suburban rail service and build rapid transit extensions.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17) The MBTA purchased the Old Colony mainline between Boston and Braintree in 1965 for the construction of the Braintree Branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)").[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-20) Contraction of the New Haven's Boston commuter service largely ended after 1967; expansion of service frequency and area began in the late 1970s.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17) In 1970, following [revolts against freeways in the urban core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_revolts_in_the_United_States#Massachusetts "Highway revolts in the United States"), Massachusetts governor [Francis Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Sargent "Francis Sargent") placed a moratorium on new highway construction inside the [Route 128 beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Massachusetts/)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded [Southeast Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Expressway_/(Massachusetts/) "Southeast Expressway (Massachusetts)") would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-problem3-21): 36 [\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-150years-17): 16  The MBTA purchased many of the Penn Central suburban lines in January 1973. These included the ex-B&P lines, the disused line from Stoughton to Whittenton Junction via Raynham, and part of the Middleborough Main Line.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-22)[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-23)[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-24) In the 1980s, the restoration of the lines to New Bedford and Fall River was proposed. Since the routes via Mansfield and Randolph and the Middleborough–Myricks segment of the Middleborough route were abandoned and built over, three possible routes to the South Coast were placed under consideration: the Stoughton route, a route following the Northeast Corridor to near [Attleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Attleboro station (Massachusetts)") and then branching onto the [Attleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attleboro_Secondary "Attleboro Secondary"), and a route following the [Middleborough Main Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_Main_Line "Middleborough Main Line") to Middleborough then the [Middleboro Secondary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleboro_Secondary "Middleboro Secondary") westwards. All three routes used the same lines from Taunton south to Fall River and New Bedford. By 1988, the MBTA was tentatively planning to extend service to Taunton via Stoughton.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-25) The first major study, completed in January 1990, concluded that the Stoughton Branch was the most viable route. The study was criticized for not considering other alternatives, including express buses.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): 1–5  A May 1991 bond bill included $3 million (equivalent to $6 million in 2024) for planning the extension.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-28) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1991agreement-29)[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-30)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-31) This included the [Middleborough/Lakeville Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_Line "Middleborough/Lakeville Line") and [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line"), which opened in 1997, plus the 2007-opened [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line").[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-netransit-32) Planning for service to the South Coast continued. The March 1995 _Expanded Feasibility Study_ analyzed routes absent from the 1990 report. The 1965–1980 construction of the Braintree Branch had only left space for a single track (intended for freight use) on the Old Colony mainline through parts of [Dorchester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorchester,_Boston "Dorchester, Boston") and [Quincy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy,_Massachusetts "Quincy, Massachusetts").[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-problem3-21): 36 [\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-clarke-33): i, 1, 4  This limited the capacity required for reaching the South Coast via Middleborough: service could be operated to one of Fall River and New Bedford, but not both.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): ii  The report concluded that both the Stoughton and Attleboro routes would be viable and that a partial [Stoughton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch "Stoughton Branch") extension to [North Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Easton "North Easton") would be most cost-effective.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1995report-26): ii [![Image 129: See caption.](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/73/Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg/250px-Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg.png)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Attleboro_Bypass_proposal_map.svg) Map of the Attleboro Bypass proposal In September 1995, the MBTA filed plans with the [Environmental Protection Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Environmental_Protection_Agency "United States Environmental Protection Agency") (EPA) for service via the Attleboro route. It was to include a 3-mile (4.8 km) 'Attleboro Bypass' on new right-of-way connecting the [Northeast Corridor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northeast_Corridor "Northeast Corridor") to the Attleboro Secondary northeast of downtown Attleboro. The project was to be completed in 2000 at a cost of $156 million (equivalent to $292 million in 2024).[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-34) In August 1996, Governor [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Weld "Bill Weld") signed a bill giving $136 million (equivalent to $250 million in 2024) to commuter rail expansion, while the state legislature directed the MBTA to further study alternatives.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) The 1997 _Expanded Alternatives Analysis_ showed vastly increased costs — $407 million (equivalent to $737 million in 2024) via Attleboro, $410 million ($742 million) via Stoughton, or $436 million ($789 million) via Middleborough. Service via Middleborough would also require double-tracking on the Old Colony mainline at additional cost. The report recommended the Stoughton route as the most cost-effective due to its high ridership.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-1997report-36) A groundbreaking ceremony was held in October 1998 after a contract for bridge work in Fall River and New Bedford was awarded that month.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-37) Based on an analysis of South Station operations, the July 1999 _Draft Environmental Impact Report_ concluded that the Stoughton route was the only viable route. It projected 4,325 daily riders with 20 trains per day to each of Fall River and New Bedford.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-38)[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-39) In January 2000, following then-governor [Paul Cellucci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Cellucci "Paul Cellucci")'s reapproval, the state reported that construction would begin in late 2002 and last until 2004.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27) The Draft Environmental Statement certificate was received in November 2000; the EPA confirmed that Stoughton was the only practical route but required a Final Environmental Impact Statement (FEIS).[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) The FEIS was released in April 2002 and approved in August. The state's approval required the Southeastern Regional Planning and Economic Development District (SRPEDD) to establish a Growth Task Force. In July 2002, the MBTA revised the project cost to $600 million (equivalent to $997 million in 2024) with an opening date of 2007.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) Due to the increasing costs, the MBTA suspended the Growth Task Force and stopped project planning in November 2002; the environmental approval process was stopped in May 2003.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) ### Restoration planning (2005–2014) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=10 "Edit section: Restoration planning (2005–2014)")\] The SRPEDD restarted the Growth Task Force in October 2004 even though the MBTA was still conducting its review of the project.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) In March 2005, Governor [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") allowed the project to proceed and allocated $670 million (equivalent to $1 billion in 2024) for the project, which was then projected to open between 2011 and 2013. The Chief of Commonwealth Development stated in June 2005 that the cost could be as high as $1 billion (equivalent to $1.5 billion in 2024).[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-timeline-27) In April 2007, the Massachusetts Executive Office of Transportation released _South Coast Rail: A Plan For Action_, which restarted the planning process from the beginning. The plan estimated project costs at $1.435 billion (equivalent to $2 billion in 2024), including $163 million ($237 million) for procuring additional rolling stock and $31.4 million ($46 million) for expanding [South Station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Station "South Station"), with opening in December 2016.[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-40) The Phase 1 Alternatives Analysis Report, released in April 2008, narrowed 65 options (including unlikely modes like [heavy rail metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rapid_transit "Rapid transit") and [monorail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monorail "Monorail")) to five plausible alternatives: the Attleboro, Stoughton, and Middleboro routes, a mixture of Attleboro and Middleboro service, and express bus service.[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-41) The [Massachusetts Department of Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Department_of_Transportation "Massachusetts Department of Transportation") (MassDOT) released 18 potential station sites for the project in September 2008.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-42)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-43) In May 2008, MassDOT issued a formal request to the [US Army Corps of Engineers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Army_Corps_of_Engineers "US Army Corps of Engineers") to allow discharge of fill materials into wetlands — effectively starting the formal environmental review process.[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-FEIS-44) A federal Notice of Intent and state Environmental Notification Form were filed in November 2008.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-srpedd-35) On October 2, 2008, the state government announced an agreement with [CSX Transportation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CSX_Transportation "CSX Transportation") for the purchase and upgrade of several of CSX's freight lines in the state. CSX agreed to sell its lines from Taunton to Fall River and New Bedford for use by the South Coast Rail project, as well as the [Grand Junction Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Junction_Branch "Grand Junction Branch"), the Framingham-to-Worcester section of the [Worcester Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Framingham/Worcester_Line "Framingham/Worcester Line"), and the [South Boston Running Track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_61_/(Boston/) "Track 61 (Boston)"). Other parts of the agreement included plans for [double-stack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-stack_rail_transport "Double-stack rail transport") freights west of Worcester and the abandonment of [Beacon Park Yard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beacon_Park_Yard "Beacon Park Yard").[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-45) The agreement was signed on September 23, 2009.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-46) On June 11, 2010, the state and CSX completed the first phase of the agreement, including the transfer of the South Coast choice, was released in September 2009.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-50) The Army Corps of Engineers released the Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) in Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whittenton_Branch "Whittenton Branch") between Raynham and Taunton was not recommended due to noise and grade crossing impacts in downtown Taunton as well as longer running times.[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-2011certificate-53) The DEIS evaluated both diesel and electric service. Electric service was projected to have faster travel times (73–76 minutes versus 83–85) due to the higher acceleration and top speed of electric trains, with higher ridership (9,580 daily riders versus 8,140) and improved air quality. However, it was projected to cost $1.88 billion versus $1.48 billion for diesel service (equivalent to $2.58 billion versus $2.03 billion in 2024), with the increased cost from the overhead wire infrastructure as well as the need to buy electric locomotives and new coaches capable of 100 mph (160 km/h) operation.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-DEIS-51): 41 [\[c\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-55) Certification from state environmental officials was received in June 2011. In the certificate, Secretary [Rick Sullivan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Sullivan "Rick Sullivan") directed MassDOT to focus on the electric alternative because it would have improved air quality.[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-56)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-2011certificate-53) A state transportation funding bill passed in July 2013 mentioned South Coast Rail as deserving funding but did not specifically allocate money to the project.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-57)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-58) In September 2013, the Army Corps of Engineers released the Final Environmental Impact Statement. It made small changes to several station sites and selected locations for layover yards. The projected cost for electric service was revised slightly downward to $1.817 billion (equivalent to $2.8 billion in 2024).[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-FEIS-44) A spending bill passed in April 2014 allocated $2.3 billion (equivalent to $3 billion in 2024) for South Coast Rail.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-59) On June 18, 2014, MassDOT awarded a one-year, $12 million contract (equivalent to $16 million in 2024) – with up to $210 million (equivalent to $273 million in 2024) possible over 10 years – to a joint venture between [Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanasse_Hangen_Brustlin,_Inc. "Vanasse Hangen Brustlin, Inc.") and [HNTB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HNTB "HNTB") for "program management, early design development, and environmental permitting".[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-60) ### Project changes (2016–2021) \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=South_Coast_Rail&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Project changes (2016–2021)")\] In June 2016, the MBTA announced that the project cost had been revised to $3.42 billion (equivalent to $4 billion in 2024), with completion not expected until 2030. The substantial delay and increase in cost caused officials to consider alternate plans, including an interim service to New Bedford via Middleborough. Some local and regional officials objected to that plan, as it would have reduced service to Middleborough/Lakeville station and potentially interfered with Plymouth/Kingston Line and Greenbush Line service.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-june2016-61)[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-62) Design for the Stoughton route was 15% complete by that time.[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-63) In March 2017, the state announced a revised plan intended to provide service sooner than 2030. The $1.1 billion Phase 1 (equivalent to $1.4 billion in 2024) would follow the Middleborough route and open in 2024; Phase 2 would follow the original route through Stoughton (including electrification) and open in 2029.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-gears-64) By June 2017, the planned completion dates were changed to Phase 1 in 2022 and Phase 2 in 2030, with stations at [Freetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freetown_station "Freetown station") and [Battleship Cove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battleship_Cove_station "Battleship Cove station") in Phase 1 rather than Phase 2 as proposed in March.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-65) The two-phase approach attracted criticism from several directions, including some of those who had previously advocated for the project as well as previous opponents.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5) Middleborough and Lakeville officials were critical of the possibility of abandoning the existing Middleborough/Lakeville station, which had attracted [transit-oriented development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit-oriented_development "Transit-oriented development"), or requiring its riders to take a shuttle train, as well as possible traffic issues from a downtown Middleborough station. The New Bedford mayor and transit advocates were critical of the longer travel times of the Middleborough routing, and the Taunton mayor was critical of Phase 1 lacking the [downtown Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton_station_/(Old_Colony_Railroad/) "Taunton station (Old Colony Railroad)") of the previous plan.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-66) Stoughton, Easton, and Raynham officials continued their previous opposition to South Coast Rail.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5) The _Draft Supplemental Environmental Impact Report_ (DSEIR) was released in January 2018. It determined that a new station would be built at [Middleborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough_station "Middleborough station") to replace Middleborough/Lakeville, and that [East Taunton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Taunton_station "East Taunton station") would be built instead of Taunton station, as serving Middleborough/Lakeville or Taunton would require time-consuming reverse moves. Battleship Cove station was moved back to Phase 2.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 19, 29  The DSEIR predicted a net increase of 3,000 daily boardings (1,500 round trips), with 2,280 daily boardings at the six new stations versus 760 at the existing Middleborough/Lakeville station.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-dseir-1): 66  The 1,610 projected daily boardings at the non-Middleborough stations were 41% of the 3,960 projected for Phase 2, leading to criticisms from public officials about the cost effectiveness of the project.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-67)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-68)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-69) The _Final Supplemental Environmental Impact Report_ was released in April 2018.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-fseir-6) Design work and permitting were largely Abandoned railbed along the Phase 2 route in Raynham The portion of the route between Stoughton and Taunton, proposed for construction in Phase 2, has proved the most controversial part of the project. While the cities of Taunton, Fall River, and New Bedford pushed for the project, the towns of [Raynham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raynham,_Massachusetts "Raynham, Massachusetts") and [Easton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Easton,_Massachusetts "Easton, Massachusetts") objected to the Stoughton route beginning in the 1990s, citing concerns about pollution, traffic, and grade crossing safety. The two towns began legal action opposing the project in 1997; [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton,_Massachusetts "Stoughton, Massachusetts") joined in 2001. Their legal fight focused on potential impacts to the [Hockomock Swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hockomock_Swamp "Hockomock Swamp").[\[113\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-116) In his 2002 approval of the Final Environmental Impact Report, Secretary of Environmental Affairs [Robert Durand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Durand "Robert Durand") mandated the construction of [a trestle through the swamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#Phase_2) to reduce impacts.[\[114\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-117) Later planning included the trestle plan.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-pineswamp-12): 4 In 2007, voters in Raynham elected to seek mitigation for impacts rather than continue litigation. Easton voters made the same choice in 2008.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-directions-118)[\[116\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-119) In 2009, Stoughton officials indicated that they would seek for a tunnel to be built through the downtown area — as was done in [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts") on the [Greenbush Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenbush_Line "Greenbush Line") — with [Stoughton station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station") moved underground.[\[117\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-120)[\[118\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-121) A town committee found that the state was unlikely to fund such a plan.[\[115\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-directions-118) In 2014, Raynham officials expressed interest in lowering tracks under [Route 138](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_138 "Massachusetts Route 138") to prevent traffic impacts.[\[119\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-122) When plans for the phased approach were announced in 2017, Stoughton, Easton, and Raynham officials continued their previous opposition to the project.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-sharp-5)[\[120\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-:9-123) Whether Phase 2 of the project will ever be built is unclear.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-finished-124)[\[122\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-125) By mid-2024, MassDOT no longer indicated that it would be built by 2030.[\[121\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-finished-124) No funding for Phase 2 was included in the MBTA's FY 2026–2030 capital investment plan in 2025.[\[123\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-126)[\[124\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-127)[\[125\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail#cite_note-128) | | The **Fall River/New Bedford Line** (formerly the **Middleborough/Lakeville Line**) is a [commuter rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commuter_rail "Commuter rail") line of the [MBTA Commuter Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MBTA_Commuter_Rail "MBTA Commuter Rail") system in southeastern [Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts "Massachusetts"), United States. It runs south from [Boston](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston "Boston") to [Taunton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taunton,_Massachusetts "Taunton, Massachusetts"), where it splits into branches to [Fall River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River,_Massachusetts "Fall River, Massachusetts") and [New Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Bedford,_Massachusetts "New Bedford, Massachusetts"). There are 10 intermediate stations on the combined section and one on each branch. With a distance of 60 miles (97 km) from Boston to New Bedford and 56.6 miles (91.1 km) to Fall River, it is the second-longest line in the system. Most of the line originated as the [Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River_Railroad_/(1846/) "Fall River Railroad (1846)"), which opened in segments between Fall River and [South Braintree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)") via Middleborough in 1845 and 1846. At South Braintree, it met the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad#Old_Colony_Railroad_\(1844%E2%80%931854\) "Old Colony Railroad"), which provided a connection to Boston. The two railroads merged in 1854 to form the [Old Colony and Fall River Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_and_Fall_River_Railroad "Old Colony and Fall River Railroad"). While the [Dighton and Somerset Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dighton_and_Somerset_Railroad "Dighton and Somerset Railroad") largely replaced the line as a Boston–Fall River route in 1866, it remained busy with commuter and Boston–[Cape Cod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod "Cape Cod") traffic. Mergers brought it under the [Old Colony Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Colony_Railroad "Old Colony Railroad") in 1872 and the [New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York,_New_Haven_and_Hartford_Railroad "New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad") in 1893. Commuter service peaked in the early 20th century and began to decline in the 1910s. Service on the Fall River–Middleborough segment ended in 1931. After two decades of attempts to end Old Colony Division service, the New Haven terminated it in 1959. Planning for the [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") to restore service on the Middleborough line began in the 1970s. Construction began in 1993, and service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line began in 1997. Seasonal [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") excursion service began using the line in 2013. The line was extended and renamed in 2025 as part of the first phase of the [South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail") project. An extension from Middleborough to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station") or [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") is proposed. Maximum speeds are 79 miles per hour (127 km/h) south of Braintree and 59 miles per hour (95 km/h) to the north.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 12 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 53  The line is mostly single track with passing sidings; there is some double track in Boston, Quincy, Braintree, and Brockton, and between Cotley Junction and Myricks Junction.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 11 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 52  Layover yards for the line are located in Fall River and New Bedford, plus an older yard in Middleborough.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 7, 47  All stations are [accessible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accessible "Accessible") with full-length high-level platforms.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-transitmatters-3): 10 [\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 56–58 As of October 2025, the portion between East Taunton and Boston has 16 round trips on weekdays and 13 on weekends.
