For the 1961 season, Boston–Cape Cod service ran via Stoughton.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 26  The New York trains ran until 1964.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-lynch-30) Freight service continued to use the Middleborough line.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 404 The [Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Transportation_Authority "Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority") (MBTA) was formed in August 1964 as an expansion of the urban Metropolitan Transit Authority into the surrounding suburbs. The MBTA was intended to subsidize commuter rail service – and to replace much of it with rapid transit extensions.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 13  The MBTA's first such project was a branch of the [Red Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Line_/(MBTA/) "Red Line (MBTA)") (Cambridge–Dorchester Line) following the Old Colony alignment to Braintree.[\[e\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-35) In November 1965, the MBTA purchased the Old Colony main line between Boston and South Braintree from the New Haven.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-36)[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 22  By 1966, the MBTA expected to eventually extend the line to Braintree Highlands or Holbrook on the Middleborough line, with a spur to [Weymouth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weymouth,_Massachusetts "Weymouth, Massachusetts") or [Hingham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hingham,_Massachusetts "Hingham, Massachusetts").[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 24  The Red Line opened to [Quincy Center station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") in September 1971 and [Braintree station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Braintree_station_/(MBTA/) "Braintree station (MBTA)") in South Braintree in March 1980.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36  Within Boston, a single freight track paralleled the new tracks. Although there was no freight service through Quincy, a single-track right-of-way was reserved for future freight use when the extension was built.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): i, 1, 4 The New Haven Railroad merged into [Penn Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penn_Central "Penn Central") at the end of 1968.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 15  In 1970, following [revolts against freeways in the urban core](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Highway_revolts_in_the_United_States#Massachusetts "Highway revolts in the United States"), Massachusetts governor [Francis Sargent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Sargent "Francis Sargent") placed a moratorium on new highway construction inside the [Route 128 beltway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_128 "Massachusetts Route 128"). The resulting cancellation of the [Southwest Expressway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southwest_Corridor_/(Massachusetts/)#Highway_proposal "Southwest Corridor (Massachusetts)") by the [Boston Transportation Planning Review](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Transportation_Planning_Review "Boston Transportation Planning Review") meant the already-overcrowded Southeast Expressway would continue to be the only highway into Boston from the south.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 36 [\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 16  In January 1973, the MBTA acquired most of Penn Central's suburban lines around Boston, including the Middleborough line as far south as Campello.[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-37)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-38)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-39) [![Image 132: A passenger train crossing a high girder bridge over a river](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a5/MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg/250px-MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MBTA_Commuter_Rail_train_on_George_L._Anderson_Bridge_November_2025.jpg) A major part of the Old Colony Lines restoration was the George L. Anderson Bridge over the Neponset River. A 1974 state report evaluated potential service as far as Hyannis and Falmouth on Cape Cod. It estimated construction costs of $13.6 million to $23 million (equivalent to $67–113 million in 2024), plus $9.2 million ($45 million) for purchasing the tracks and $2.5 to $6.8 million ($12–34 million) for equipment.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-40) On October 15, 1979, a special train ran from Braintree to Middleborough to publicize the state's plans for restored service.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-secondsection-41) In 1984, a state-directed MBTA study found that restoration of commuter rail service on the former Old Colony lines would be feasible.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4  During the summers of 1984 to 1988, the [Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_and_Hyannis_Railroad "Cape Cod and Hyannis Railroad") operated passenger service between Braintree station and Cape Cod. Intended partially as a precursor to full commuter rail service, it made five intermediate stops (Holbrook, Brockton, Bridgewater, Middleborough, and Wareham) between Braintree and Buzzards Bay.[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-43)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-anew-44)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-45) A Draft Environmental Impact Statement (DEIS) for restoration of service on the Middleborough, Plymouth, and Greenbush lines was released in May 1990.[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-46) In 1991, the state agreed to build a set of transit projects as part of an agreement with the [Conservation Law Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservation_Law_Foundation "Conservation Law Foundation") (CLF), which had threatened a lawsuit over auto emissions from the Central Artery/Tunnel Project ([Big Dig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Dig "Big Dig")). Among these projects was the "Old Colony Commuter Rail Line Extension", to be complete by the end of 1996.[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1991agreement-47)[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-48)[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-49) The Final Environmental Impact Statement for the Middleborough and Plymouth lines – often called the "Old Colony Lines" – was released in 1992.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-50)[\[f\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-51) Two station sites considered in the DEIS – Westdale in West Bridgewater and Middleborough/[Route 44](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Route_44 "Massachusetts Route 44") in northern Middleborough – were dropped from consideration.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 4 Construction of the $560 million project began in 1993, with service then expected to begin in late 1996.[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-52) Which stations to include on the shared mainline between Braintree and Boston proved controversial. Original plans called only for a stop at Braintree.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 8  In September 1995, state governor [Bill Weld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Weld "Bill Weld") announced that a platform would be built at [Quincy Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Center_station "Quincy Center station") instead.[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-53) Later that year, the MBTA agreed to build both stations.[\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-54) In November 1996, the MBTA agreed to add a stop at [JFK/UMass station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JFK/UMass_station "JFK/UMass station") as well.[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55) Limited weekday service with four daily round trips each on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line and [Plymouth/Kingston Line](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plymouth/Kingston_Line "Plymouth/Kingston Line") began on September 29, 1997.[\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-56)[\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-57) Full service began on November 30, 1997. The Middleborough/Lakeville Line had twelve round trips on weekdays and seven on weekends.[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-58)[\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-59) Weekend and some weekday trains began stopping at JFK/UMass on April 30, 2001.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5)[\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-bypass-55) [![Image 133: A diesel locomotive leading a passenger train into a suburban station with a curved high-level platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7b/Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station%2C_Lakeville_MA.jpg/250px-Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station%2C_Lakeville_MA.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Outbound_train_entering_Middleborough-Lakeville_MBTA_station,_Lakeville_MA.jpg) A train at Middleborough/Lakeville in 2013 In 2007, [concrete ties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concrete_sleeper "Concrete sleeper") used on the Old Colony Lines began to fail due to manufacturing errors. The rate of failures increased during the following two winters, affecting service and causing speed restrictions.[\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-60) In 2010, the MBTA began a project to replace the 150,000 failing ties, which were part of a batch of 600,000 made in the 1990s, with wooden ties.[\[g\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-62) Some replacement work in Bridgewater and Middleborough took place in 2010.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-beacon-ties-61) Midday service on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line was replaced by buses from March 14 to June 6, 2011.[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63)[\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-64) Weekend service on the line was replaced from March 26 to December 18, 2011, and March 17 to April 22, 2012.[\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-65)[\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june1-63) The project was completed in May 2012 at a cost of $91.5 million.[\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-66)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-67) On May 24, 2013, the MBTA began operating [CapeFlyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CapeFlyer "CapeFlyer") service between Boston and Hyannis over the Middleborough Main Line and Cape Main Line. Service consisted of one daily round trip on Friday evenings, Saturdays, and Sundays during the summer tourist season.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[\[h\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-70) In 2013 and 2014, the Friday evening southbound train operated as an extension of a regular Middleborough/Lakeville Line train, while Saturday and Sunday service operated with a separate trainset. In 2015, Friday CapeFlyer service also began using a separate trainset.[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-capeflyer2013-68)[\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-71) Substantially reduced schedules were in effect on the Commuter Rail system from March 16 to June 23, 2020, due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5) Schedule changes effective November 2, 2020, added midday service with consistent 60-to-70-minute midday headways on the Middleborough/Lakeville Line, though a pilot of late-night service was discontinued.[\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-72) Temporary reduced schedules were again put into place from December 14, 2020, to April 5, 2021.[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-73)[\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-74) By October 2022, Middleborough/Lakeville service was at 77% of pre-COVID ridership.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-oct2022ridership-1) [![Image 134: A curved high-level railway station platform](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8e/Middleborough_station_near_completion_%281%29%2C_August_2023.jpg/250px-Middleborough_station_near_completion_%281%29%2C_August_2023.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Middleborough_station_near_completion_/(1/),_August_2023.jpg) Middleborough station near completion in August 2023 In the 1980s — during the first expansion of commuter rail service in Massachusetts in decades — the restoration of service to New Bedford and Fall River ([South Coast Rail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Coast_Rail "South Coast Rail")) was proposed. Three routes were considered, including the Middleborough Main Line and Middleborough Secondary. By 1988, the MBTA was tentatively planning to use a route via [Stoughton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_station "Stoughton station").[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-75) A 1995 feasibility study found that the limited capacity of the single track between Boston and Braintree could only support service to Fall River or New Bedford, but not both.[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1995report-76) Planning for the Stoughton route continued until it was suspended in 2003.[\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-srpedd-77) Planning restarted several years later. The 2009 alternatives analysis report, 2011 draft [environmental impact statement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impact_statement "Environmental impact statement"), and 2013 final environmental impact statement all chose the Stoughton route.[\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-78)[\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-DEIS-79)[\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FEIS-80) In June 2016, the MBTA announced that the project cost had been revised to $3.42 billion, with completion not expected until 2030. The substantial delay and increase in cost caused officials to consider alternate plans, including an interim service to New Bedford via Middleborough. Some local and regional officials objected to that plan, as it would have reduced service to Middleborough/Lakeville station and potentially interfered with Plymouth/Kingston Line and Greenbush Line service.[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june2016-81)[\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-82) In March 2017, the state announced a revised plan intended to provide service sooner for a total cost of $3.42 billion. The $1.1 billion Phase 1 would follow the Middleborough route and open in 2024 with service to both Fall River and New Bedford. Phase 2 would follow the Stoughton route (including electrification) and open in 2029.[\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-gears-83) Middleborough and Lakeville officials were critical of the possibility of abandoning Middleborough/Lakeville station — which had attracted [transit-oriented development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transit-oriented_development "Transit-oriented development") — or requiring its riders to take a shuttle train.[\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sharp-84) By June 2017, the Phase 1 completion date was moved to 2022.[\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-85) The draft supplemental environmental impact report was issued in January 2018. It analyzed three options for Middleborough: a reverse move to serve the existing station, a new Middleborough station with a rail shuttle between the existing station and Bridgewater, and a new Middleborough station with a bus shuttle from the developments at the existing station site. The third option was chosen for higher operational flexibility, lower travel times, and avoiding the need to add double track between Middleborough and Bridgewater.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 19 The two main construction contracts for the project were awarded in May and August 2020. By then, service was expected to begin in late 2023.[\[78\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-FRaward-86)[\[79\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-87) Overall project completion reached the halfway point in mid-2022.[\[80\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-88) In September 2023, the MBTA indicated that revenue service would not begin until mid-2024.[\[81\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-89) In April 2024, the MBTA acknowledged that a midyear opening was unlikely but did not provide a new schedule.[\[82\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-90)[\[83\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-91) In June 2024, the MBTA announced that the planned opening had been delayed again to May 2025.[\[84\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-92)[\[85\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-93) Service began on March 24, 2025. The line was renamed as the Fall River/New Bedford Line at that time.[\[86\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-march24-94)[\[87\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-95) Weekday service on the main portion of the line increased from 14 round trips to 16; weekend service increased from 10 round trips to 13.[\[88\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-scr-schedule-96)[\[89\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-97) The months after the extension saw several service quality issues.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) A shortage of rail crews caused some trains to be cancelled during the first several weekends.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98)[\[91\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-99) The MBTA preemptively replaced some trips with buses on the weekends of April 19–20 and 26–27.[\[92\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-100)[\[93\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-101)[\[94\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-102) One third of trains were late during the first two weeks of extended service, versus one-tenth systemwide. On-time performance improved thereafter but remained below the rest of the system through April and May. The MBTA blamed "startup conditions" and difficulty coordinating trains on the mostly-single-track line for the issues.[\[90\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-june5-98) On July 21, 2025, the schedule was changed to improve reliability. This included removal of off-peak and weekend stops at JFK/UMass, removal of two late-night shuttle trains, and longer running times.[\[95\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-103)[\[96\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-104) By November 2025, daily ridership on the line was about 2,000 higher than a year before.[\[97\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-105) ### Cape Cod service proposals \[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line&action=edit§ion=11 "Edit section: Cape Cod service proposals")\] [![Image 135: A Spanish revival style railway station](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9d/Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg/250px-Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Buzzards_Bay_station_HDR.jpg) [Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station"), a possible future terminus of service In 2007, the Boston Region Metropolitan Planning Organization released a feasibility study of extending commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay,_Massachusetts "Buzzards Bay, Massachusetts"), a portion of [Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne,_Massachusetts "Bourne, Massachusetts") on the north side of the [Cape Cod Canal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Cod_Canal "Cape Cod Canal"). Intermediate stops were to be at Rock Village in southern Middleborough, County Road on the [Rochester](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rochester,_Massachusetts "Rochester, Massachusetts")/[Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham,_Massachusetts "Wareham, Massachusetts") border, and [downtown Wareham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wareham_Village_station "Wareham Village station").[\[98\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2007study-106) The introduction of the CapeFLYER brought new attention to the possibility of extending the Middleborough/Lakeville Line to Buzzards Bay.[\[99\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-possibility-107) Later in 2013, the Wareham Chamber of Commerce and Buzzards Bay town selectmen both indicated support for Buzzards Bay commuter rail based on the success of the CapeFLYER, the Chamber supported the extension of commuter rail service to [Buzzards Bay station](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buzzards_Bay_station "Buzzards Bay station").[\[100\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-108)[\[101\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-109) [MassDOT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MassDOT "MassDOT") and the Cape Cod Commission both studied the potential service in 2014–15. The studies estimated daily ridership of 800 to 875 if all Middleborough/Lakeville trains were extended to Buzzards Bay without intermediate stops.[\[102\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-2015study-110) Bourne voted to join the MBTA district in 2015 and began paying an [assessment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_assessment "Tax assessment") in mid-2016, although there was no guarantee that commuter rail service would be provided.[\[103\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-111) MassDOT began planning a possible trial service in October 2015. The service was to have shuttle trains between Bourne and Middleborough/Lakeville operated by [Massachusetts Coastal Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Coastal_Railroad "Massachusetts Coastal Railroad").[\[104\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-rausch-112) The MBTA Fiscal Management and Control Board rejected the service proposal in April 2016.[\[105\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-113) During the South Coast Rail project, Middleborough station was designed with space for a shuttle platform to be added later.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-dseir-2): 38  In 2021, MassDOT released a feasibility study of Cape Cod commuter rail service. Middleborough–Buzzards Bay shuttle service with seven daily round trips was expected to have 1,710 total daily boardings, while Middleborough–[Bourne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bourne_station "Bourne station") service with ten daily round trips (including two off-peak Boston round trips) was expected to have 2,540 total daily boardings. Service to Hyannis was not evaluated because the Bourne–Hyannis segment would require significant track and signal improvements to be suitable for commuter service.[\[106\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-114) 1. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-8)** Until August 1846, its name was the United Corporation of the Middleborough Railroad Corporation with the Fall River Branch Railroad Company and the Randolph and Bridgewater Railroad Corporation.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-sne-6): 403 [\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-7) 2. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-12)** The Boston–Braintree main line was double-tracked in 1848; the northern portion was quadruple-tracked in the early 20th century.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 95  3. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-17)** Two trains used the West Bridgewater Branch and [Stoughton Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stoughton_Branch "Stoughton Branch"); one used the [Bridgewater Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Bridgewater_Branch&action=edit&redlink=1 "Bridgewater Branch (page does not exist)") and the Plymouth main line. Six additional trains operated from Bridgewater to Boston using the Bridgewater Branch.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 34, 96  4. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-23)** Those on the Middleborough line were Matfield, Westdale, and Stanley – all between Brockton and Middleboro. [Rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station#History "Middleborough/Lakeville station"), [South Middleboro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middleborough/Lakeville_station#History "Middleborough/Lakeville station"), and [Tremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tremont_station_/(Massachusetts/) "Tremont station (Massachusetts)") were all between Middleborough and Wareham.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-wouldclose-22)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem1-20): 19  5. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-35)** Part of the Cambridge–Dorchester Line had previously been constructed along a section of the main line plus the [Shawmut Branch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shawmut_Branch_Railroad "Shawmut Branch Railroad") in the 1920s.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-150years-11): 96  A rapid transit extension to Braintree had been proposed by regional plans in 1926 and 1945.[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-1926report-33)[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-34) That plan was overwhelmingly rejected by Quincy and Braintree voters in 1948.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem2-27): 10–12  Not until Old Colony service ended did the plan gain traction.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 29 [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-clarke-32): 1  6. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-51)** Unlike the other two lines, the Greenbush Line involved reactivation of abandoned right-of-way, and it proved more controversial. The MBTA moved forward with the Middleborough and Plymouth lines; after significant controversy, the Greenbush Line ultimately opened in 2007.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-ES-42): 5 [\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-problem3-28): 37 [\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-netransit-5) 7. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-62)** [Amtrak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amtrak "Amtrak") and the [Long Island Rail Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_Island_Rail_Road "Long Island Rail Road") also had to replace large numbers of ties from that batch.[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-beacon-ties-61) 8. **[^](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-70)** For the 2013 season, the service ran until [Columbus Day](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbus_Day "Columbus Day") weekend in mid-October.[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_note-permanent-69) 1. ^ [_**a**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-oct2022ridership_1-0) [_**b**_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_River/New_Bedford_Line#cite_ref-oct2022ridership_1-1) Poftak, Steve (October 27, 2022). Updated March 24, 2025, 8:30 a.m. ET

*   South Coast Rail, the MBTA's commuter rail connection from Boston to Fall River and New Bedford, is now open for business.
*   The passenger rail extension was 34 years in the making and cost $1.1 billion.

_(This story was updated to accurately reflect the most current information.)_

Passenger rail service has been restored to Fall River and New Bedford for the first time in nearly 67 years — [the South Coast Rail to Boston](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/02/11/mbta-issues-south-coast-rail-updates-on-service-scheduling/78399168007/) is now officially open for business.

Multiple decades in the making, [the MBTA’s Middleboro/Lakeville Line has now been renamed the Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/commuter-rail). It extends from Boston south to Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford, connecting the SouthCoast’s three largest cities to the state capital by train for the first time since 1958.

In New Bedford, well over 100 people waited at the station before dawn to witness the first train of the new Fall River/New Bedford Line leaving the station at 4:27 a.m. The new pedestrian bridge spanning Route 18 aglow behind them, people were buttoned up against the early morning's chill, but warm with excitement. Most were there to mark the occasion, including Ruhaan Sharma-Soneja, who said he had also seen the opening of the MBTA's Green Line extension in 2022.

![Image 1: The first MBTA commuter rail train out of New Bedford gets ready to leave the station at 4:27 a.m. on Monday, March 24, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/24/NHER/82632399007-train-1.jpg?width=660&height=495&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Penny Brewer of Fairhaven, holding a homemade sign reading “Bon Voyage,” said she first heard about plans to re-establish train service to Boston in the 1970s and has been waiting ever since.

“It’ll be good for the town,” she said.

James Abreu, originally of Tyngsboro but a UMass Dartmouth student, sported a red sweatshirt with the T logo across the front. He described himself as a railroad enthusiast.

“It’s definitely a historical moment,” he said. “It’s truly something special.”

[![Image 2](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/24/NHER/82632398007-train-3.jpg?crop=2047,1153,x0,y231&width=660&height=372&format=pjpg&auto=webp)](https://www.heraldnews.com/picture-gallery/news/2025/03/24/first-mbta-commuter-rail-trains-leave-new-bedford-and-fall-river/82632432007/)

Fall River sees its first train departure, with MBTA's biggest fan watching
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Fall River’s first train at 5:05 a.m. drew a crowd, including Mayor Paul Coogan and state Rep. Carole Fiola — and many enthusiasts to see it off.

Chris Aguiar of Fall River, who lives in Worcester now, made sure to wake up early just to be able to say he took the first ride.

![Image 3: Chris Aguiar of Fall River checks the MBTA commuter rail map at Fall River Depot station, in preparation for the first 5:05 a.m. departure on Monday, March 24, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/24/NHER/82632402007-train-4.jpg?width=660&height=614&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

“I grew up in Fall River, 30-some-odd years,” he said. “I always had an interest in trains. Never having a train down here stunk.”

He and many others held out their phones, snapping shots and capturing video of the historic occasion, with no bigger enthusiast than Kolson Miller, 9.

“The MBTA has been the most biggest, biggest, biggest, biggest thing for me and I love it so, so much,” Kolson said. “I loved it since I was 5 or 6 years old. ... This is the most exciting day of my life.”

He wasn’t taking a ride just yet — he had school later that morning. In his hands he clutched his phone, capturing video for YouTube, and swag handed out by South Coast Rail project managers witnessing the first departures. Kolson said he has his future career lined up, an unsurprising choice.

“I’d want to be an MBTA conductor,” he said.

![Image 4: A passenger settles into a seat aboard the 5:05 a.m. MBTA commuter rail train out of Fall River Depot on Monday, March 24, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/24/NHER/82632400007-train-6.jpg?width=660&height=517&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

South Coast Rail: Six new stations, weekday and weekend service 
----------------------------------------------------------------

The MBTA’s Fall River/New Bedford Line project required the construction of six new passenger platforms: Fall River Depot, Freetown, New Bedford, Church Street, East Taunton and Middleboro.

Along with those are two layover stations, in Fall River and New Bedford, where trains are docked overnight.

[The MBTA’s fee structure puts all stations into Zone 8](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/04/mbta-free-south-coast-rail-weekend-rides-all-the-details/81219478007/) — $12.25 for a one-way ticket all the way to Boston’s South Station, or $6 if paying reduced fare. The schedule has trips about every 70 minutes during the week, and every two hours on weekends.

[In a 2022 interview](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2022/10/12/south-coast-rail-fall-river-commuter-station-90-percent-mbta/8237500001/), South Coast Rail spokesperson Jean Fox said she estimated the train would carry 1,610 riders a day from Fall River and New Bedford, taking them off traffic-choked expressways. A ride from end to end will take about 90 minutes.

![Image 5: An MBTA train rolls through the East Taunton commuter rail station on March 20, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/20/NHER/82570312007-t.jpg?width=660&height=381&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Gov. Baker: 'We are excited for the rail line to bring more visitors here'
--------------------------------------------------------------------------

The commuter rail line arrives both a year and a half late, yet also over a month early.

Initially planned to open in late 2023, a miscalculated safety testing schedule caused project managers to punt the long-delayed project [to mid-2024](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2023/09/29/south-coast-rail-mbta-moves-commuter-service-to-24-for-safety-checks/70997274007/) and [eventually to May 2025](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/06/13/mbta-ceo-south-coast-rail-delayed-to-may-2025-fare-unveiled/74092923007/). MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng announced earlier this year that safety testing had been concluded more quickly than anticipated, bringing the start of revenue service to late March.

![Image 6: The new East Taunton commuter rail station is open to passengers.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/20/NHER/82570332007-t-2.jpg?width=660&height=444&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

The project's history spans seven state governors — but South Coast Rail, as currently built, was set in motion by the administration of then-Gov. Charlie Baker in 2017.

Aboard the first train in Fall River, Fiola noted that though many officials deserved thanks, Baker deserved a special “pat on the back for being able to see the need brought to him that we could do this.”

“He made that last push before this administration,” Fiola said.

Baker himself, in a statement to _The Herald News_, noted that he made the rail a priority of his tenure.

"After years of unfulfilled promises, our administration was the first to take South Coast Rail from theory to action and we fully funded a realistic construction plan that is now operating," Baker said. “New Bedford, Fall River and all SouthCoast communities are Massachusetts treasures, and we are excited for the rail line to bring more visitors here and make it easier for the people of the SouthCoast to travel to Greater Boston."

![Image 7: State Senator Mark C. Montigny gives the train conductor a thumbs up as it makes its way past the Whale's Tooth train station in New Bedford during a test run, before service begins next week.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/24/mbta-south-coast-rail-to-fall-river-new-bedford-starts-rolling/82627178007/)

Train history: Passenger rail once thrived in SouthCoast, taken over by cars
----------------------------------------------------------------------------

The $1.1 billion project is one of the largest, most extensive infrastructure projects on the SouthCoast in recent history — and perhaps the longest to come to fruition.

Passenger trains once crisscrossed the state as part of the Old Colony Railroad system, operated by the New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad company. For almost a century until the mid-20th century, the company commonly known as the New Haven Railroad dominated transportation in southern New England.

But by the late 1950s, facing multimillion-dollar losses, and as trends shifted to greater automobile ownership and the building of more interstate highways, the railroad system’s operator struggled.

New Haven Railroad discontinued service to Fall River, New Bedford and Taunton after July 8, 1958.

![Image 8: State Senator Mark C. Montigny looks at the train lines leading in and out of the city as he checks in on the commuter train during a test run to the Whale's Tooth train station in New Bedford, before service begins Monday, March 24.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/24/mbta-south-coast-rail-to-fall-river-new-bedford-starts-rolling/82627178007/)

It continued passenger service elsewhere on the Old Colony network, floated by state subsidies, before abandoning it entirely a year later.

At a February 2025 public meeting, state Sen. Michael Rodrigues of Westport acknowledged the change in transportation trends, and how things have swung back.

“With the Post World War II boom in highway development and the changes of transportation priorities throughout the United States of America, our commuter rail system fell apart,” Rodrigues said. “But here we are again.”

![Image 9: State Rep. Carole Fiola, D-Fall River, looks out for friends boarding the first MBTA commuter rail train out of Fall River Depot on Monday, March 24, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/03/24/NHER/82632397007-train-5.jpg?width=660&height=495&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Seven governors and $1.1 billion later 
---------------------------------------

South Coast Rail was first envisioned in 1991 during the term of then-Gov. William Weld as an extension of the MBTA’s Commuter Rail line from Stoughton. He expressed such confidence that it would be built under his tenure that in February 1992 he proclaimed, “Sue me if it doesn’t happen.”

Politicians promised riders at least nine different deadlines from 1997 to 2024, with the price tag rising from $136 million to $1.1 billion — and [over $3 billion if a proposed "Full Build" with electric trains through Taunton to Stoughton ever materializes.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/07/10/south-coast-rail-what-is-the-full-build-and-will-it-be-constructed/74346910007/) The project remains conceptual and largely unfunded. MBTA's website, which once estimated the Full Build for 2030, no longer includes a timeline.

Even in its limited form, the project spanned the terms of six U.S. presidents, seven governors, five New Bedford mayors, seven Fall River mayors, and eight Taunton mayors.

“I’ve literally been working on this project for close to 30 years, where we’ve had so many promises, to once again connect Fall River and New Bedford, two hub cities of the SouthCoast, to Boston via commuter rail,” Rodrigues said.

Aboard the train in Fall River on Monday, Fiola said building the project was a group effort including not just legislators and politicians but everyone.

“If this community, along with New Bedford, did not push as hard as everyone in the same direction, this would not have happened,” Fiola said. “If everybody wants it, if everybody is pushing, that’s how we get things done.”

New Bedford Had Commuter Rail Service to Boston Once Before
===========================================================

[Barry Richard](https://wbsm.com/author/barryrichard/)

[Barry Richard](https://wbsm.com/author/barryrichard/)Published: July 25, 2023

Townsquare Media

*   [Share on Facebook](http://www.facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Fwbsm.com%2Fnew-bedford-commuter-rail-boston-before%2F%3Ftrackback%3Dfbshare_mobile "Share on Facebook")
*   [Share on Twitter](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?text=New%20Bedford%20Had%20Commuter%20Rail%20Service%20to%20Boston%20Once%20Before%20http%3A%2F%2Fwbsm.com%2Fnew-bedford-commuter-rail-boston-before%2F%3Ftrackback%3Dtwitter_mobile%20%40WBSM1420 "Share on Twitter")

As New Bedford prepares to welcome the arrival of daily commuter rail service from Boston this fall, questions remain about whether it can be successful given that most of us have become accustomed to driving ourselves these days, and whether enough people are willing to spend upwards of 90 minutes each way to commute between here and there.

I suppose we are about to find out.

New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell recently told me that the restored rail service should not be viewed as a commuter rail service since, in his opinion, the number of folks who will use it for that purpose will likely be low.

Mitchell said train service between New Bedford and Boston will most likely be for occasional day trippers.

New Bedford-Boston Passenger Train Service Ended In 1958

Barry Richard/Townsquare Media

For decades. SouthCoast politicians have demanded a rail link to Boston, declaring it a matter of "economic justice." With New Bedford gradually establishing itself as a regional hub with less dependence on Boston, some wonder if the need for the rail project is somehow less than before.

![Image 3: WBSM-AM/AM 1420 logo](https://townsquare.media/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/WBSMAM.png?w=100)

Get our free mobile app

Commuter rail service between New Bedford and Boston was first established in 1885 by Old Colony Railroad.

Old Colony Railroad, which operated from 1845 until 1893, covered Southeastern Massachusetts and parts of Rhode Island. Old Colony ran trains from Boston to Plymouth, Fall River, New Bedford, Newport, Providence, Fitchburg, Lowell and Cape Cod.

The company also operated steamboat and ferry lines, including the Fall River Line.

New York, New Haven and Hartford Railroad acquired the Old Colony Railroad in 1893. The Old Colony division discontinued passenger service by 1959, except for the main line between Boston and Providence.

All passenger service between New Bedford and Boston ended on September 5, 1958.

Governor Healey, MBTA Announce Free South Coast Rail Weekend Service and Parking Through April
==============================================================================================

Posted on February 26, 2025
---------------------------

Governor Maura Healey and the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) have announced free weekend service and parking to celebrate the beginning of South Coast Rail service. The MBTA is on schedule to begin [South Coast Rail](https://urldefense.com/v3/__https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail__;!!CPANwP4y!WOhk-NSgU6qmVzP4YDsOiEi9SNC4bXvgnObDN3qTeeKAaU1pL4UY2Oq_Ao6hhO2yVSGzy9ezec5eNxkcCW5z$) passenger service the morning of March 24, 2025, pending final FRA approval. This will be the first time the region has had passenger rail service in 65 years. A schedule will be released next week.

"We are so excited to be less than a month away from the launch of South Coast Rail service. This will make it easier for South Coast residents and visitors to move around the state, reduce congestion, support local businesses and spur new housing and economic development," said **Governor Maura Healey**. "To celebrate the launch and encourage people to try out this new service, we are proud to be offering free weekend travel and free parking throughout March and April."

"South Coast Rail is a gamechanger for the South Coast and our entire state. Our administration is all about making it easier, quicker and more affordable for folks to get where they need to go," said **Lieutenant Governor Kim Driscoll**. "We're grateful to General Manager Eng and his team at the T for delivering this major project, and we encourage everyone to check it out and take advantage of free weekend travel and parking."

“The Healey-Driscoll Administration is committed to expanding access to public transportation, investing in infrastructure improvements, and furthering the mission of MassDOT to provide safe, reliable and resilient transportation in every corner of the state,” said **Transportation Secretary and CEO Monica Tibbits-Nutt**. “We are excited about the beginning of passenger rail service between Fall River, New Bedford, and Boston on March 24 and know that several weeks of free parking and weekend free fares at select properties are just the incentive needed to boost ridership.  The new train service and discounts will transform how people travel into the city from communities on the South Coast.”

"The MBTA is proud to bring rail service to the Southeastern communities after 65 years, offering new and exciting opportunities for residents and visitors in this region," **said MBTA General Manager and CEO Phillip Eng**. "Providing free weekend service and parking through April is something we are pleased to offer riders to encourage more people to experience the convenience of this valuable transportation expansion. We will continue to invest in the Commonwealth’s communities and provide mass transportation service that the public deserves and expects.”

**Free Weekend Service**

Fare-free service will be available on South Coast Rail’s Fall River and New Bedford lines for all weekends (Saturdays and Sundays) between March 29 and April 27, and on April 21 (Patriots’ Day). Passengers can ride for free if they are boarding or ending their ride at one of the six South Coast Rail stations.

Riders should share their origin and destination stations with conductors in order to receive free travel. This offer is only valid on the Fall River and New Bedford lines and does not apply to trains on other Commuter Rail lines.

**Weekday Fare Information: Regular Commuter Rail Fares Apply**

On weekdays, regular Commuter Rail fares are in effect for South Coast Rail. All South Coast Rail stations will be priced in Zone 8. This means that passengers will pay a full fare of $12.25 and a reduced fare of $6 for a one-way ride between Zone 1A to 8.

Other Fare Options:

*   **Weekend/Holiday Pass:** Flat $10 weekend and holiday pass fares apply across Commuter Rail stations and zones including South Coast Rail 
*   **Monthly Pass (Zone 8):** Monthly Zone 8 passes cost $388 full fare / $190 reduced fare. A discount of $10 full fare / $5 reduced fare is available for monthly passes on mTicket.  

**Free Parking**

Commuter Rail parking at the six South Coast rail station lots – Middleborough, East Taunton, Freetown, Church Street, Fall River Depot, and New Bedford – will be free March 24 through the end of day April 30, 2025.

This free parking promotion may end early if South Coast Rail parking lots fill up and spaces become unavailable. Standard parking rates for South Coast Rail stations are $4 per day on weekdays and $2 per day on weekends/holidays.

For more information, visit mbta.com/SouthCoastRail.

See the initial release [here](https://www.mass.gov/news/governor-healey-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-weekend-service-and-parking-through-april).

Commentary

*   October 17, 2025
*   [Commuter/Regional](https://www.railwayage.com/category/passenger/commuterregional/)

Written by [David Peter Alan](https://www.railwayage.com/author/davidpeteralan/), Contributing Editor

![Image 1: image description](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Outbound_MBTA_New_Bedford_train_2021_and_Fall_River_train_1971_at_East_Taunton_March_2025_1.jpg)

Outbound MBTA New Bedford Line train #2021 (left), and Fall River shuttle train #1971 (right, providing a timed connection to #2021), at East Taunton station. Wikimedia Commons/4300streetcar

**Usually when passenger service on a rail line is discontinued, it never comes back, but there have been some exceptions. One is the [MBTA’s South Coast Rail](https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail) “line,” in the shape of the letter “Y,” going from Boston to the two outer destinations of New Bedford and Fall River, Massachusetts. The route was historically part of the Old Colony Railroad, and later the New Haven, branching westward from the main (now Amtrak’s NEC) at Canton Junction. The old New Haven served New Bedford and Fall River until 1958, and passenger trains on the rest of the Old Colony lines bit the dust shortly after.**

On March 24 of this year, service from Boston’s South Station returned under the auspices of the “T” for the first time in 66 years, with 36 miles of track rebuilt. As part of my effort to catch up on all the “new starts” in the United States and Canada, including lines that have returned to service, I rode from Boston to New Bedford on Tuesday, October 7 and back from Fall River the next day.

Service returned under the MBTA (the “T”) as part of Boston’s regional rail system, operated by Keolis. The operation is unusual, because of the shape of the line. The operation is not like the Northside line on Boston’s North Shore, where alternating trains go either to Rockport or Newburyport, with essentially “double service” to inner suburbs like Salem and Beverly. Instead every train runs between South Station and either New Bedford or Fall River. Shuttle trains serve the other destination from a transfer station in East Taunton, about a 75 or 80-minute ride from Boston. There are slightly more trains that serve New Bedford than Fall River 15 or 14 on weekdays and seven or six on weekends. Saturday and Sunday schedules are the same.

While the operation is interesting, the line is not scenic, and the stations are not placed conveniently for visiting the towns, which are interesting and normally have plenty of things to see and do.

The Line
--------

![Image 2](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/TRN_MBTA_South_Coast_Rail-619x1024.jpg)

**_MBTA_**

The current line is not the original route to New Bedford and Fall River. Rather it is a longer line where service is operating for several years on a temporary basis. There are presently unfunded plans to restore service in the future through Easton and Taunton on the former line that was abandoned south of Stoughton, which is two stops south of Canton Junction. In the meantime, the trains now run on the former Middleborough-Lakeville Line, on newly upgraded track the rest of the way to the transfer point and the destination cities on the New Bedford Main or Fall River Branch from Myrics Junction. The route to Fall River essentially follows the original 1846 route of the Old Colony & Fall River RR.

Passenger trains were absent from the entire Old Colony system (except between Providence and Boston, which is now part of the NEC) from 1959 until the present Kingston (and also a short branch to a Plymouth station that was not close to the center of town) and Middleborough-Lakeville Lines opened for restored service in 1997. Because of local opposition and other issues, the Greenbush Line did not get new passenger service for another ten years. The South Coast routes extend the former Middleborough-Lakeville Line and run on it as far as Middleborough. Today the Lakeville station is used only for the seasonal _Cape Flyer_ train to Hyannis on summer weekends, although there has been talk of running peak-commuting trains as far as Buzzards Bay, just short of the Cape Cod Canal and the famous lift bridge that carries the _Cape Flyer_ and local freight trains over the canal.

From South Station, the trains run along the right-of-way of the Red Line subway on a surface-running segment through Quincy to Braintree. They do not serve Back Bay Station. The only current station located in a downtown area is Brockton, although the Bridgewater station is within walking distance of downtown and Bridgewater State, the local college. The next stop after Middleborough is East Taunton, where cross-platform transfers are available. I rode the 6:45 AM departure, the first train of the morning. It was bound for Fall River, so it was necessary to change trains for New Bedford.

The ride between Boston and the outer ends is scheduled to take roughly 1¾ hours, although my train was not due into New Bedford until 8:47. The trainset that was supposed to leave Boston consisted of both single-level cars (two types) and bilevel cars, a mix found only on the T. Due to mechanical issues, all riders were sent to an all-bilevel consist on a dfferent track, which delayed our departure by 15 minutes. Still, there was enough slack in the schedule that we arrived at New Bedford at 8:43. On the way there, there is a station at Church Street, in the northern part of town.

![Image 3](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/2025-03-24-south-coast-rail-east-taunton-opening-1024x576.jpg)

_**MBTA**_

The Towns
---------

New Bedford and Fall River have much in common, and a single day was only enough time to get the flavor of each of them. Both towns are historic, and both pride themselves on their maritime history. New Bedford has two maritime museums: the New Bedford Whaling Museum (which requires all day to see in detail) and another operated by the National Park Service, which was closed due to the federal government shutdown when I was there. The town also has an active waterfront, with ferries, fishing boats, and some freight-carrying boats. Fall River also has a maritime museum and a waterfront but, instead of major commercial activity, there is Battleship Cove, which is now home to the battleship _USS Massachusetts_ and other vintage Navy ships that are now tourist attractions.

The cities are similar in population: New Bedford has slightly more than 100,000 residents, which Fall River has slightly less than that number. Both cities have highly diversified populations, due in large part to their industrial and seafaring histories. Mills are still standing in both places, and some have been repurposed for commercial or residential use. In addition to immigrants who came to this country to work in the mills, many islanders from the Azores, the Cape Verde Islands, and Madeira formed the large Portuguese communities in both towns. There are also Italian, various Hispanic, other European, and Asian communities. New Bedford was founded by Quakers, and the Black community there has historic roots. Frederick Douglass lived there for a few years around 1840. The diversity in both cities also gave rise to a varied food scene, consisting mostly of locally owned, independent restaurants.

Another feature that the destinations have in common is that the train stations are not located in convenient places. The New Bedford station is about a half-hour walk north of the city center. The mapping software on my tablet directed me to walk along Acushnet Avenue, a grimy industrial street named after the river that flows through the town. It might have been a better idea to walk across a new bridge from the station and over a wide highway to Purchase Street, and take a bus the rest of the way. The Fall River station is also located some distance north of downtown. There is a boardwalk and bike-and-walking trail along the waterfront that goes to the station, but there are presently no wayfinding signs, so access is tricky. There is a proposal to extend the line to Battleship Cove in the future.

Both towns are historic, but their histories are somewhat different.

New Bedford
-----------

New Bedford is a beautiful, historic city. Its primary industry in the middle of the 19th century was whaling, although other maritime trades were practiced there, and industry later supplanted maritime trade. Herman Melville spent time in town and used it as the setting for _Moby_ Dick, his classic novel about whaling, which was published in 1851. Many of the old buildings along the waterfront have been preserved, and they are now filled with shops and eateries that cater to tourists as well as locals.

Downtown New Bedford appears to have changed little in the past 100 years, and many century-old (or older) commercial and government buildings are well-kept and still serve their original purposes. The interior at City Hall (originally the library) dates from the early 1900s and features a semicircular elevator surrounded by an old-fashioned cage, run by an operator, and furnished with a bench for the comfort of the passengers making the 20-foot journey between the first and third floors. The residential parts of County Street and other nearby neighborhoods feature an eclectic mix of houses of different Victorian styles, as well as those from a century ago. While the town has its rough spots, there appears to be enough to see and do for an inquisitive tourist to keep busy for three or four days of sightseeing. So, there is still plenty to see and do in New Bedford, especially if the local history museum reopens (which could happen before the end of this year). One of the activities is finding the train station.

Fall River
----------

Fall River is as historic as New Bedford, but not as upscale. There are historic buildings downtown, and the classic library, whose slogan: “The People’s University” is carved into its facade, is one of the most beautiful. More buildings in Fall River have been unsympathetically altered, while more in New Bedford retain their historic accuracy. Still, Fall River has some neighborhoods with historic houses, like New Bedford’s, too. Fall River does not have as large a historically upscale component as New Bedford. Traditional New England “triple-decker” houses, with a different family living on each floor, are common throughout Massachusetts, and they abound in Fall River.

![Image 4](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/hqdefault-1024x576.jpg)

**_Fall River Chow Mein Sandwich, a genuine culinary atrocity_**

As in New Bedford, there are several Portuguese restaurants, and the food in the Portuguese communities in Massachusetts is different than that found in the other major Portuguese community in the Northeast: The Ironbound in Newark, N.J.. The other local food specialty is the “Fall River _Chow Mein_ Sandwich,” an example of an unfriendly meeting of East and West found in local Chinese restaurants. If you are used to authentic _chow mein_ from a big-city Chinatown (with pan-fried noodles to give them a chewier texture than _lo main_ noodles have) you won’t find it in Fall River. What you will find is the bottom of a slider-sized hamburger bun with a handful of crisp noodles taken from a bag and placed on top. The noodles are then topped with a brown gravy whose color and saltiness come from a generous amount of soy sauce. The top have of the bun is placed alongside, and the concoction is eaten with a fork, not chopsticks. If you are not from Fall River, you might consider it a genuine culinary atrocity. I did, but I spent $5.00 to try it so you don’t have to.

![Image 5](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Lizzie_Borden_1890-1024x576.jpg)

**_“Lizzie Borden took an ax and gave her mother 40 whacks… when she saw what she had done, she gave her father 41. Andrew Borden is now dead, Lizzie hit him on the head, up in heaven he will sing, on the gallows she will swing.”_** **_Borden was acquitted._**

Fall River also has a local obsession: Lizzie Borden and the 1892 murders of her father and stepmother. [The house where the murders took place is still standing, and today it operates as a combination inn and tourist attraction.](https://lizzie-borden.com/) For $30.00 you can take a tour of the house, which will include the basement, where the murder weapon (an axe) was found, for an additional $7.00. For a few hundred, you can stay there, if you have always wanted to spend the night in the place where two of the most infamous murders in American history took place. Lizzie was acquitted (some local buffs believe that her privileged background helped produce that result), and she managed to stay in the area and keep her lifestyle going until she died in 1927. The building next door to the infamous house on Third Street is now home to Lizzie’s, a combination art gallery and coffee shop, where the coffee is good and Lizzie is still the main topic of conversation.

Back to Boston
--------------

![Image 6](https://www.railwayage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/gallery-south-coast-rail-10-1024x576.jpg)

**_HNTB_**

Because I was booked to go home on Amtrak train 179 (7:47 PM form South Station), I had to catch the 4:41 train from Fall River. It ran through to Boston and connected with a shuttle from New Bedford. Part of the line through Fall River is elevated, so it’s possible to get a last look at the town on the way to Boston, including a brief glimpse of the ships in Battleship Cove on the waterfront. There is one station between Fall River and the East Taunton transfer station: Freetown, about a ten-minute ride inbound. Freetown is the home of a large nature park, but it is not visible from the train.

For this writer, the ride back was a good way to learn more about the railroad form Assistant Conductor Aden Walker, a second-generation railroader whose father is an engineer on the system. He pointed out the interlockings, stretches of single track, and other features of the route as we rode. There are four callouts needed to dispatchers on different parts of the route, ending with Terminal Dorchester, which covers all Amtrak and local trains that serve South Station, as well as other services. Our train was running against the heart of the commuter peak, and we had six meets along the way. Most of the route is rated for 79 mph, but with a 30-mph restriction at Bridgewater. We arrived at South Station at 6:23. Part of the fun during the ride was learning about the route from a young railroader who was following a family tradition and looking forward to a long career on the rails.

The fare between Boston and either New Bedford or Fall River is $12.25 each way, $6.00 for seniors and people with disabilities. There is a lot to see in both cities, and it’s not necessary to take the train to East Taunton and transfer to a train going to the other destination. The Southeastern Regional Transit Authority (SRTA) runs local buses in both cities, with a route between them that runs local service and express buses that run on the highway and take 25 minutes between the two downtown terminals. Buses run until about 9:00 on weekdays, but only from mid-morning until late afternoon on weekends.

There is a lot to see in both towns, especially when the museums are open. It was more pleasant than taking a bus would have been, and riding on a route that has been restored after a decades-long absence is something to celebrate. The towns are closer to Providence than Boston, but trains from Providence don’t go to New Bedford or Fall River, only to Boston and the suburbs on the way there.

REMINDER: Red Line Braintree Branch Will Be Suspended Between North Quincy and Braintree November 15 – 23
=========================================================================================================

Posted on November 10, 2025
---------------------------

**This notice serves as a reminder of the upcoming Red Line Braintree Branch closure** [**previously announced on October 20**](https://www.mbta.com/news/2025-10-20/mbta-announces-november-service-changes)**.**

* * *

The MBTA is today reminding riders that Red Line Braintree Branch service will be suspended between North Quincy and Braintree for nine days, November 15 – 23.

![Image 1: Shuttle stops and closed stations for the Red Line closure](https://cdn.mbta.com/sites/default/files/styles/max_2600x2600/public/media/2025-10/2025-11-15-red-line-north-quincy-braintree-diversion-diagram.png?itok=OmRt9NGl)

The MBTA will continue essential infrastructure upgrades, track renewal, and other critical revitalization work on the Red Line. Building on the success of the Track Improvement Program, this regular, planned renewal and revitalization work is ongoing and continuous, ensuring the long-term stability of our infrastructure and preserving the system for future generations of riders.

During this service change, crews will accomplish major rail revitalization work throughout the affected area with critical full-depth track replacement work and signal modernizations at the Quincy Center crossover, which is an area of complicated track that connects the main Braintree Branch to subway car storage track areas nearby. Crews are also maximizing the unencumbered access to the area by advancing many other critical projects, like security system upgrades, bridge project work and inspections, and station enhancements and deep cleaning. When service resumes following this service change, riders will experience an even more reliable trip on the Red Line with fewer disruptions due to older infrastructure and outdated signals. This work is also critical to maintaining consistent 50 MPH service on the Braintree Branch and supports the MBTA’s goal of further reducing trip times for riders.

Riders can find complete information at [mbta.com/RedLine](http://www.mbta.com/RedLine). More information on these service changes and alternate travel options is below:

*   Free and accessible shuttle bus service will replace trains between North Quincy and Braintree.  
     
    *   Riders using shuttle bus service should budget ample extra travel time. For example, a rider travelling to Park Street from Braintree should budget at least an additional 35 minutes of travel in addition to their regular commute.  
         
*   Riders are strongly encouraged to use the [Fall River/New Bedford](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-NewBedford/timetable), [Kingston](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Kingston/timetable), and [Greenbush](https://www.mbta.com/schedules/CR-Greenbush/timetable) Commuter Rail lines for fare-free service between Braintree, Quincy Center, JFK/UMass, and South Station. Commuter Rail schedules are available on [mbta.com/CR](https://www.mbta.com/CR).  
     
    *   Commuter Rail trains operate about every 20 – 30 minutes.  
         
    *   Extra coaches will be added to the Fall River/New Bedford, Kingston, and Greenbush Commuter Rail lines to accommodate the anticipated increase in ridership.  
         
    *   Riders should note that regular Commuter Rail fares will be collected for travel beyond Braintree.  

More information is also available through in-station signage and public announcements. Transit Ambassadors and MBTA staff will be available on-site to offer information and assistance during these service changes. Riders are encouraged to [subscribe](https://alerts.mbta.com/) to [T-Alerts](https://www.mbta.com/alerts) or to follow the MBTA on X [@MBTA](https://twitter.com/mbta) for up-to-date service information.

More Information
----------------

Media Contact Information
-------------------------

For questions or comments about this press release, please contact:

MBTA Media Relations

[MediaRelations@mbta.com](mailto:MediaRelations@mbta.com)

[857-368-8500](tel:+1-857-368-8500)

Members of the press can request to join our media list by emailing [MediaRelations@mbta.com](mailto:MediaRelations@mbta.com). We'll send you MBTA press releases and media advisories directly.
