Updated Sept. 23, 2016, 4:59 p.m. ET

![Image 1: Tracks split at Myricks. The right leg heads to Fall River through Freetown and the center track continues to New Bedford. The track turning to the left is an industrial siding.](https://www.heraldnews.com/gcdn/authoring/2016/09/23/NHER/ghows-WL-22c6acef-b977-42ce-9183-8bbda67dfe15-32ac5de2.jpeg?width=660&height=479&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

FALL RIVER – Virtually three months since state transportation officials suddenly revived a dormant [South Coast Rail](http://www.massdot.state.ma.us/southcoastrail/Home.aspx) limited connection through Middleborough, hundreds of people have weighed in on whether a sudden change in direction for the commute to Boston adds up.

From the first five of six regional public forums held this month, including in the southern triangle of cities Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford, roughly 400 people attended of which 328 signed in and 110 of the participants asked questions or gave opinions to Massachusetts Department of Transportation and MBTA officials, Jean Fox confirmed.

MassDOT’s South Coast Rail project manager Jean Fox, preparing for the final forum held Thursday in Middleborough, said, “In the next several weeks our goal is to really synthesize those comments.”

Fox will work with Nancy Farrell, who’s moderated and whose Boston public affairs consulting firm has been compiling every comment, including dozens of emails, to bring concrete responses to MassDOT Secretary Stephanie Pollack, she said.

The MassDOT/MBTA position is pursuit of the so-called new Middleborough option — in conjunction with the established Stoughton route — is dependent upon public opinion that translates into a consensus of local and state elected officials in the South Coast Rail territory.

Fall River’s forum on Sept. 14 elicited overall support to pursue this Middleborough option, with varying levels of certainty and a range of questions to be answered.

Fall River Mayor Jasiel Correia II reacted ecstatically to the prospect at the state’s public forum at Bristol Community College.

“Middleborough is the only route I see to getting rail to the SouthCoast,” said Correia, who brought others from his administration to drive home how critical the economic and related benefits of rail would be for Fall River.

**Price tag comparisons coming**

Pollack and MBTA General Manager Frank DePaola raised consideration of rail service through the existing Middleboro/Lakeville line to their Fiscal Management and Control Board three months ago based on dramatically changed cost and construction time estimates through Stoughton, they said.

The new $3.4 billion cost had grown, they said, more than $1 billion from previously announced figures, and MassDOT now lists a projected completion date of 2030. That is seven to nine years longer than various estimates given previously.

That’s about twice as long as estimated in January 2013, when the price tag was $1.8 billion or close to half the price pegged early this summer.

Despite the fact ranking state officials since the June 27 Middleborough announcement have been publicly stating much shorter construction durations and lower costs, Jim Eng, MassDOT Administrator of Transit Rail, has asserted those figures for a Middleborough route are premature.

“If we develop a conceptual design, we’ll know better how much the costs are and what it will take,” Eng said prior to the final forum in Middleborough.

Eng said determining “the extent of wetlands mitigation” would be critical to design and costs. The decision on pursuing that design will be made in the upcoming weeks, officials said.

**Technical data this winter**

Their engineering joint-venture partner, VHB/HNTB, hired in 2014, reported if given the go-ahead they’d complete a technical analysis of the cost, duration, ridership, environmental process and infrastructure needs by this winter for public assessment.

([Read the full presentation here](https://drive.google.com/file/d/0BxwqxJQAhe0tVWNjV3Z1X21iMGU4VXpiaW5fWk96ZWlmb0Nv/view?usp=sharing).)

The 7½-mile Middleboro alternative route on existing track requiring upgrading and able to handle limited trains would go east from Cotley Junction in Taunton. That’s south of Taunton’s downtown and the station design for a Stoughton route, and is a source of criticism from Taunton officials that envision economic benefits greatly diminished.

Sen. Marc Pacheco, D-Taunton, has attended every forum to advocate for continued pursuit of the Stoughton route that is 30 percent designed within the southern triangle and 15 percent north of his city.

He said a Middleborough train from this area was rejected three times before, the “numbers always change” and “I don’t have any faith in them.”

While the state explores technical analysis for Middleboro, it would continue to pursue design and pre-permitting for the preferred Stoughton route of 52 miles and 75 and 77 minutes, respectively, from Fall River and New Bedford to South Station, officials said.

Stoughton was firmly established as the choice route and having the least environmental impact in June 2013.

At that time, state officials under Gov. Deval Patrick’s administration projected the cost of South Coast Rail at $1.4 billion with a completion date of 2021, eight years.

Precisely a year later in June 2014, Patrick, in his final year of two terms, announced the 10-year, $210 million engineering design contract awarded to VHB/HNTB, and said South Coast Rail and the preferred route through Stoughton had become a “game changer.”

_Listen to former Gov. Deval Patrick talk about the Stoughton route in 2013._

**State leaders said 5-6 years to build**

That was based upon imminent prospects of changing from a “planning” to a “construction” stage. The project cost was estimated at $2.3 billion, the state’s listed cost until three months ago.

Under the long-assumed project design, the commuter trains would run 20 trips from both Fall River and New Bedford with projected daily ridership of about 4,500.

Primarily because of the competition for track use to South Station, MassDOT has said two peak morning and two peak evening trains would come and go from Fall River and New Bedford through Taunton to Middleborough, and a few others at off-peak hours.

Eng, responding to the public’s recommendations, said, “We’d look at whether we can do three” at peak times.

On costs, Rep. William Strauss, D-Mattapoisett, co-chairman of the joint transportation committee, told The Herald News shortly after the state announcement in June they believe the Middleborough route could be operating in six years and cost at least $1 billion less than the one through Stoughton.

Similarly, When Lt. Gov. Karyn Polito addressed a business group in Dartmouth in mid-July, speaking in concert with Gov. Charlie Baker, she said Middleborough could be built in a period “closer to five years,” versus the “15 to 20 years” for one through Stoughton.

She noted much of the infrastructure was already in place.

Initial estimates have been it would take 14-15 minutes longer because of the longer route and use of slower diesel trains versus the electric trains planned through Stoughton.

According to media reports, state officials rejected previous options through Middleborough because of insufficient track capacity on the existing Old Colony line.

A few months ago transit officials re-examined that route after receiving an informal offer that could lead to expanding the Southeast Expressway in Dorchester to accommodate more rail lines, Wicked Local Newsbank previously reported.

**Lang says 2 years to build, less than $300 million cost**

Among those most vocal supporting Middleborough has been Scott Lang, the former New Bedford mayor who’s advocated and researched this alternative’s consideration for a decade.

He believes it would take “probably two years” to build this route, and the wetlands permitting of a half-dozen communities in the southern triangle could begin soon with 30 percent design achieved.

Lang said he believes costs including the limited number of diesel trains should be no more than $250 million.

Lang was told what Eng said about the Army Corps’ position just a month ago relating to completing the rail south of Taunton without the entire project reaching the 30 percent design that typically triggers construction.

“What the Army Corps said to us is unless you finish 30 percent design in the northern portion, they will not allow us to build anything in the southern triangle,” Eng said.

“I believe that the Army Corps will work with the state on Middleborough,” Lang said.

“We have to let them know that the project can commence building in the southern portion, and the northern portion is not contemplated in the near future,” Lang recommended.

He believes MassDOT/MBTA has to take “the official position” construction can’t begin in the southern area “while they’re hearing what the public has to say … I think they wanted to make sure if they committed to the Middleborough route that they’d have support of the public. And I think they have support of the public.”

Added Lang, “It’s time to focus on reality – there’s no way to justify building a single-shot rail for $3.4 billion.”

Fox was asked about the 10-year, $210 million engineering contract the state awarded two years ago, and what would happen if the administration decides to pursue Middleborough.

“The scope would change, no question about that,” said Fox, who’s been South Coast Rail project manager the past five years.

That direction would be part of the decision making this winter, she said.

**Partnership seeks budget, detailed time line**

More than two-dozen people spoke at the Fall River forum and several others gave their reactions to the presentation after being contacted.

Hugh Dunn, executive director of the SouthCoast Development Partnership at the University of Massachusetts Dartmouth, said he is looking for a detailed time line and budget if Middleborough is pursued.

He thinks providing three trains to each coastal city at peak hours is important.

Dunn, whose organization of business, non-profit and educational leaders this summer supported exploring Middleborough while continuing to work toward design and permit completion of Stoughton, said he’d like to see “notice of a project change by the end of the year” — if that’s the state’s intention.

He was encouraged by the condensed public forums this month to expedite the process.

“Should we really take an in-depth look?” is the question his organization wants the state to answer sooner rather than later.

He’s encouraged that despite understandable “rail fatigue” the Fall River delegation “is on the same page.” He also thinks the new administration “wouldn’t breathe energy into the project unless they really meant to do it.”

“It may be that Middleborough is the long-term solution, or a near-term solution, while Stoughton is the long-term route,” said Josh Ostroff, interim director of Transportation for Massachusetts, a coalition that voted to endorse South Coast Rail in 2015.

**Gov. Baker intervene?**

The Stoughton line permitting must be completed before any construction in the southern triangle begins, Ostroff said, and changing that requirement “will likely require intervention by Gov. Baker.”

“Advocates for rail service are criticizing alternative routes based upon impatience, which is understandable. But it is counter-productive to oppose any solution until we have all the facts,” said Ostroff, who assumed his organization’s leadership after Kristina Egan moved to another position in Portland, Maine.

Egan, former South Coast Rail project manager, had strongly criticized the state when it announced its new approach.

She said the Stoughton route was the only permissible option to pursue after the Army Corps called it the “least environmentally damaging practicable alternative” in 2012, which remains operative, Wicket Local reported.

“This proposal really represents a false hope to stakeholders in Fall River and New Bedford. If Gov. Baker wants to kill this project, he should be honest and face the consequences,” Egan said at the meeting when Pollack and DePaola made the announcement for a Middleborough option.

Among Fall River residents that spoke out, Tom Lowney of Mount Hope Avenue in the South End, said his family has lived in the city for several generations. A ship fitter for Electric Boat after 20 years’ service in the Navy, Lowney said he looked forward to retirement and taking trips by train to Boston with his wife and two grown children.

He moaned over driving up on a Friday, saying wistfully he “can’t just get on the train and go.”

Lowney said he thought South Coast Rail was “on an even keel with the previous governor,” and is perplexed by the time to build it now reportedly doubling.

He sees Middleborough “not as a complete alternative line but as a temporary alternative line.”

He makes a comparison: “If we treated the highway system like this, we’d still be in the stone age.”

Lowney plans to write his opinions to MassDOT by its Sept. 30 deadline.

“The Rail to Boston Coalition supports Middleborough in conjunction with Stoughton continuing,” said Tim Cole, its vice chairman.

“I can’t see how we can’t pursue it,” said Cole, like Dunn stating his coalition of business and community groups wants to see a budget and time table soon.

**Worcester did it**

He thought City Administrator Cathy Ann Viveiros “hit the right note” at the forum by urging the state to expedite rail to start accruing its benefits. “The time factor really matters,” Cole said.

A graduate of B.M.C. Durfee High School – where his grandfather Ambrose Keeley had been principal – and having obtained multiple graduate degrees after commuting by vehicle to attend Boston University for his bachelor’s, Cole said rail is the engine to drive the local economy.

Like others did, he used the example of Worcester starting with a few trains and now sporting about 20 as ridership continued to grow.

“The same thing could happen here,” Cole said. “Make it happen. Get the rail here.”

South Coast Rail will incorporate “Middleborough Route”
=======================================================

![Image 47: image description](https://www.rtands.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/09/42132075b2c1020dc5a262944f268200.jpg)

MBTA

**The Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT) is planning to construct the South Coast Rail project in two phases, beginning with the Middleborough Route.**

MassDOT filed a Notice of Project Change (NPC) for the [South Coast Rail (SCR) Project](http://www.massdot.state.ma.us/southcoastrail/Home.aspx) with the Massachusetts Environmental Policy Act (MEPA) Office on March 15, 2017. MassDOT says taking a phased approach to construction and utilizing the existing Middleborough/Lakeville Commuter Rail Line will provide service sooner than if the project was constructed all at once.

“Our administration is committed to providing the South Coast with commuter rail service as expeditiously and efficiently as possible,” said Massachusetts Gov. Charlie Baker. “Pursuing the Middleborough/Lakeville early action service while advancing the Stoughton Electric final phase service will facilitate commuter rail service to the region years earlier.”

The 7.5-mile Middleborough Secondary Line, which must be upgraded to handle commuter rail traffic. While the MEPA review is underway, MassDOT will advance work on the so-called Southern Triangle, from Cotley Junction in Taunton south through Berkley, Lakeville, Freetown, Fall River, and New Bedford, which is common to both the early action and final phases of the project.

The first phase of the project would extend and upgrade the existing Middleborough/Lakeville Line via the 7.5-mile Middleborough Secondary Line, which provides a quicker, less expensive option for service to and from New Bedford and Fall River. Trains heading towards the South Coast would then join the New Bedford Main Line and continue to New Bedford or branch off on the Fall River Secondary to Fall River. Phase 1 service would be diesel, as the existing Middleborough Line does not include the overhead catenary required for electric service. Phase 1 would also include the construction of several new stations and layover facilities in the Southern Triangle.

As the early action service is permitted and implemented, MassDOT would continue to advance design of the Stoughton Electric Phase 2 of the SCR Project. This phase consists of new track, signals and stations between Canton Center and Cotley Junction.

“We are pleased to continue advancing the South Coast Rail Project and working towards providing commuter rail service to the South Coast region in a timely and efficient manner,” said Transportation Secretary and CEO Stephanie Pollack. “This Notice of Project Change allows MassDOT to analyze impacts and incorporate public input of the proposed change to develop this project in phases. This will enable us to provide passenger rail to the South Coast region years sooner than would be the case if the project were constructed at one time.”

New Bedford Port Authority to share parking lot with MBTA, Seastreak ferry: How it works
========================================================================================

The Standard-Times

USA TODAY NETWORK

March 19, 2025, 4:06 a.m. ET

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=302658364351205&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.southcoasttoday.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F03%2F19%2Fnew-bedford-mbta-station-seastreak-ferry-parking-at-whales-tooth-lot%2F82526182007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.southcoasttoday.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F03%2F19%2Fnew-bedford-mbta-station-seastreak-ferry-parking-at-whales-tooth-lot%2F82526182007%2F&text=New%20Bedford%20Port%20Authority%20to%20share%20parking%20lot%20with%20MBTA%2C%20Seastreak%20ferry%3A%20How%20it%20works&via=southcoasttoday)[](mailto:?subject=New%20Bedford%20Port%20Authority%20to%20share%20parking%20lot%20with%20MBTA%2C%20Seastreak%20ferry%3A%20How%20it%20works%20-%20from%20New%20Bedford%20Standard-Times&body=New%20Bedford%20Port%20Authority%20to%20share%20parking%20lot%20with%20MBTA%2C%20Seastreak%20ferry%3A%20How%20it%20works%0A%0AThe%20Whale%E2%80%99s%20Tooth%20parking%20lot%2C%20operated%20by%20the%20New%20Bedford%20Port%20Authority%2C%20will%20provide%20both%20MBTA%20and%20Seastreak%20parking.%20Here's%20what%20to%20know.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20southcoasttoday.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.southcoasttoday.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F03%2F19%2Fnew-bedford-mbta-station-seastreak-ferry-parking-at-whales-tooth-lot%2F82526182007%2F)

Keep Watching

*   The Whale's Tooth parking lot in New Bedford will share space for both the MBTA and Seastreak ferry.
*   The lot will have 150 spaces set aside for MBTA users only, with 570 for the ferry riders.
*   There will be some fee changes, and the payment system will be text-based.

NEW BEDFORD — The Whale’s Tooth parking lot at 532 Acushnet Ave. will begin using a new payment system for parking to accommodate MBTA rail passengers [when commuter rail service begins](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/12/mbta-commuter-rail-questions-dogs-tickets-bathrooms-food-and-more/82285343007/), while continuing to serve the lot’s primary use of hosting Seastreak Ferry passengers.

For the past several years, the Whale’s Tooth lot, owned and operated by the [New Bedford Port Authority](https://portofnewbedford.org/), has been used exclusively by the [Seastreak seasonal ferry service operator](https://seastreak.com/what-to-know/port-locations-directions-parking/new-bedford-ma/) for passenger parking, according to a press release.

Under an agreement with the MBTA, the Port Authority will designate 150 spaces for MBTA passengers on the northern end of the lot closest to the new train station. The remaining 570 spaces will be dedicated to ferry parking. There will be no advanced or reserved purchase of parking. All parking will be first come, first served.

Take a free ride: [How will South Coast Rail's free weekends work? Do you need a ticket? Everything to know.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/04/mbta-free-south-coast-rail-weekend-rides-all-the-details/81219478007/)

![Image 1: A passenger train makes a test run on the soon-to-open commuter rail line ending at the Whale's Tooth station in New Bedford.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/19/new-bedford-mbta-station-seastreak-ferry-parking-at-whales-tooth-lot/82526182007/)

Parking lot will use a new payment system
-----------------------------------------

The Whale’s Tooth Lot will use a gateless text-to-pay fare system for parking. While the XPressPark system will not be the same as at other MBTA-owned and managed lots, which use the PayByPhone app, it will function in much the same way.

10 common questions: [Can you take a dog on South Coast Rail? Are there bathrooms on board?](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/12/mbta-commuter-rail-questions-dogs-tickets-bathrooms-food-and-more/82285343007/)

The system will provide clear information on parking rates, with payments made and verified through a text interface.

There will be two different parking rates to address the different users. The day rate will match the same rate charged by the MBTA at the lots it owns and operates along the Fall River/New Bedford Line: $4 per day on weekdays, $2 per day on weekends.

[How to get to Fenway Park from South Coast Rail: 10 places in Boston to visit via transit](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/lifestyle/2025/04/16/boston-tourist-guide-via-public-transit-visiting-via-south-coast-rail/83086632007/) [Can you take a dog on South Coast Rail? Are there bathrooms on board? 10 common questions](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/12/mbta-commuter-rail-questions-dogs-tickets-bathrooms-food-and-more/82285343007/) [For students, seniors and low-income, rail has discounts. Who qualifies and how to apply.](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/02/19/mbta-commuter-south-coast-rail-reduced-fares-who-qualifies-and-how-to-apply/79114621007/) [SRTA to roll out MicroConnector: Book a ride to New Bedford, Fall River train stations](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/28/srta-microconnector-app-shuttle-service-south-coast-rail-stations-fall-river-new-bedford-ma/82708811007/) [Did MBTA underpay for Weaver's Cove in Fall River? Jury to decide eminent domain lawsuit](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/) [MBTA hears South Coast Rail reliability, noise complaints: 'We want to regain your trust'](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/business/transportation/2025/06/06/mbta-hears-south-coast-rail-complaints-over-noise-unreliability/84062523007/) [These MBTA commuter rail schedule changes could reduce night-time noise, make trips faster](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/business/transportation/2025/07/10/mbta-south-coast-rail-schedule-changed-to-reduce-nighttime-noise/84538811007/)

![Image 2](https://www.southcoasttoday.com/story/news/2025/03/19/new-bedford-mbta-station-seastreak-ferry-parking-at-whales-tooth-lot/82526182007/)

Because most of the Whale’s Tooth lot will be used by Seastreak Ferry passengers who typically park for extended periods, there will be a multi-day rate of $15 charged to any vehicle parked beyond the daily hours of the MBTA service. Overnight/multi-day parking is generally not allowed in MBTA-operated lots, so this rate is designed for ferry passengers and is the same rate they paid for the past several years.

The XpressPark text-to-pay system will alert parkers twice before their parking time expires. There will be options to add multi-day fees before the ticketing enforcement begins.

Daily parking free through April 30
-----------------------------------

While the Whale’s Tooth lot will generally operate differently than other MBTA lots, to align with the MBTA’s promotional program at all of its stations along the new line, daily parking will be free through April 30. The multi-day parking fees will begin with the start of Seastreak’s seasonal service on April 17.

Ferry and rail passengers can also park in the Elm Street parking garage in downtown New Bedford, 51 Elm St., a short walk to the train station and ferry terminal.

For more information and frequently asked questions visit the NBPA website at [portofnewbedford.org](http://portofnewbedford.org/).

54.content:
_By Jeff Stagl, Managing Editor_

In early February, the Massachusetts Coastal Railroad (MCRR) got a bit larger. That’s when the short line officially acquired the assets of Bay Colony Railroad (BCLR).

Under a purchase agreement, MCRR acquired the permanent freight easement to 35 miles of track that was operated by BCLR. Now, MCRR has expanded to operate 132 route miles of track and control an additional 44 miles of track owned by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation (MassDOT).

MCRR will manage BCLR’s daily operations. Last year, MCRR applied to the Surface Transportation Board for approval of the transaction and was granted a favorable decision in December. As the track owner, MassDOT was consulted throughout the purchase process.

Established in 1982, BCLR served North Dartmouth and Millis in southeastern Massachusetts. Launched in 2008, MCRR provides integrated freight-rail and logistics services throughout the South Coast of Massachusetts and southern New England, and interchanges with CSX. The short line now manages nearly 176 miles of track stretching from Framingham to Fall River, and New Bedford to Hyannis.

The acquisition was an important step forward in providing efficient and environmentally friendly freight-rail service in Massachusetts, said MCRR President and CEO Chris Podgurski in an email.

![Image 1: Mass Coastal 2](https://www.progressiverailroading.com/resources/editorial/2024/mass-coastal-2-900x500.jpg) Mass Coastal now operates 132 route miles of track and manages an additional 44 miles of track owned by the Massachusetts Department of Transportation. Massachusetts Coastal Railroad

“Interestingly enough, these line segments are basically what’s left of the original Bay Colony Railroad,” he said. “It makes sense for the Mass Coastal to pick up these lines, as it makes the most commercial sense to protect the customers and guarantee their connections to national rail system going forward.”

MCRR has built a strong relationship with CSX and MassDOT’s rail unit, Podgurski adds. The short line partners with the unit, Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority (MBTA) and CSX to provide a crucial rail connection to the national rail network that extends into Canada and Mexico.

“Bay Colony \[served\] three customers in Dartmouth and Westport, \[which\] positioned us to acquire some additional rail users, as well,” Podgurski said. “The Bay Colony properties will enhance our freight shipping capabilities on behalf of Massachusetts businesses and residents.”

MCRR plans to continue advocating for the preservation and expansion of transit rail in Massachusetts. The railroad’s lines are used for the CapeFlyer passenger-rail service and Cape Cod’s Polar Express Train in addition to industrial freight shipping in the Cape Cod area. Operated by the Cape Cod Regional Transit Authority in collaboration with the MBTA and MassDOT, the CapeFlyer runs between Boston and Cape Cod.

### Making freight rail more viable in Maryland 

Meanwhile, the Western Maryland Scenic Railroad (WMSR) recently acquired a dormant rail line in southwestern Allegany County — which had operated as the Georges Creek Railway — through a lease agreement. The scenic railroad has re-branded the line as its Georges Creek Division, which is structured as a separate business managed by WMSR.

The railroad signed a 36-month lease with the line’s owner, Eighteen Thirty Group LLC. The lease will enable the railroad to diversify and expand, and pursue various revenue streams, including both passenger- and freight-rail opportunities, WMSR officials say.

Over the past three years, WMSR has doubled the number of riders on its excursion options between Cumberland and Frostburg, Maryland. The railroad operates four-season excursions, dinner trains, family holiday-themed events and The Polar Express Train Ride.

Also, CSX and various vendors over the years have occasionally approached the scenic railroad about providing limited freight-rail service that’s better suited to a detail-oriented short line rather than a large Class I, said WMSR Executive Director Wesley Heinz in an online post. WMSR provided some freight-rail service in 2021 but had limited space — particularly at its yard in Ridgeley, West Virginia — to handle more of the traffic. Now, the Georges Creek Division will provide additional freight access, said Heinz.

![Image 2: WMSR](https://www.progressiverailroading.com/resources/editorial/2024/WMSR-900x500.jpg) The Western Maryland Scenic Railroad recently acquired a dormant line, which now is re-branded as its Georges Creek Division. The railroad aims to develop freight-rail business on the line. Western Maryland Scenic Railroad

“Our staff has spent countless hours imagining a revitalization of the railroad line and how WMSR can use their vision to bring economic development to the Georges Creek Valley through tourism and rail services,” he said.

In 2006, the Eighteen Thirty Group and Georges Creek purchased the historic Georges Creek line out of bankruptcy, intending to maintain it. The previous railroad had provided rail and switching services for the former Verso paper mill in Luke, Maryland, but the railroad ceased operation in 2019 when the mill closed.

Since 2021, WMSR has proposed multiple concepts to sustain the line’s potential, Heinz said. Now, the first order of business is addressing overgrown vegetation along the right of way, identifying safety needs and working with community leaders to encourage and diversify tourism throughout the Georges Creek Valley, he said.

Maintenance work is required on the track to restore service, and portions of the line could be operational by late 2024. A main portion in need of repairs: a 400-foot stretch of track in Moscow that was washed out by a flood in 1996.

When South Coast Rail starts up on March 24, MBTA commuter rail trains will roll into two new stations in New Bedford. This guide will show you how to get to them, no matter how you decide to travel. New Bedford Station is northeast of downtown, sharing a parking lot with the Seastreak Ferry. Church Street Station is in the North End, southeast of Kings Highway. ![Image 5](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/TODs2-ig.jpg?resize=780%2C921&ssl=1) ![Image 6](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/TODs2-ig2.jpg?resize=780%2C920&ssl=1) ### **On foot** The most pedestrian-friendly route to **New Bedford Station** is the brand-new [pedestrian bridge](https://newbedfordlight.org/ask-the-light-whats-that-big-arch-over-rt-18-in-new-bedford/) from Purchase Street. It sits between Pearl and Willis streets, and arches across Route 18 directly to the station. If you’re starting from the eastern side of Route 18, there are sidewalks along MacArthur Drive and Acushnet Avenue leading to the station. The path to **Church Street Station** is a little more straightforward. If you can make your way to Church Street, sidewalks will guide you to the station. ### **On a bicycle**  Use caution if you ride a bicycle to **New Bedford Station** — there are no bicycle lanes near the station on Acushnet Avenue, or on Purchase Street near the pedestrian bridge. Meanwhile, **Church Street** does have bicycle lanes on the same side of the street as the station. There are bicycle racks at both stations. See the MBTA’s website for [bike parking policies](https://www.mbta.com/bikes/bike-parking). Bicycles are allowed on South Coast Rail trains, but it’s up to the conductor’s discretion. If the train is too crowded, you might be asked to wait for the next train. More information about bringing bicycles on trains is available on the [MBTA’s website](https://www.mbta.com/bikes/bringing-your-bike-the-train). ### **In a car** The trick to reaching **New Bedford Station** is finding a way to get east of Route 18 onto Acushnet Avenue. Here’s how to get there: ![Image 7](https://i0.wp.com/newbedfordlight.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/New-Bedford-Station-test-train-scaled-b-edited.jpg?resize=780%2C437&ssl=1) ### Learn more [How do I buy tickets for the South Coast Rail?](https://newbedfordlight.org/how-do-i-buy-tickets-for-the-south-coast-rail/) ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [It’s official: South Coast Rail schedule released](https://newbedfordlight.org/its-official-south-coast-rail-schedule-released/) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [SRTA rushing to prep for South Coast Rail](https://newbedfordlight.org/srta-rushing-to-prep-for-south-coast-rail/) ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [Free weekend rides planned to lure South Coast Rail users](https://newbedfordlight.org/free-weekend-rides-planned-to-lure-south-coast-rail-users/) --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- [_Full South Coast Rail coverage ⇢_](https://newbedfordlight.org/southcoastrail/) * **From downtown, the West End, and the South End:** Make your way to MacArthur Drive by heading east on Potomska Street, Walnut Street, or Elm Street. Then turn left to head north on MacArthur Drive — it eventually becomes Acushnet Avenue. * **From the areas immediately north of downtown:** Cross Route 18 by heading east on the overpass at Hillman Street and turning left onto Acushnet Avenue. * **From the North End:** Make your way to Logan Street by heading south on Purchase Street or North Front Street. Then, head south on Acushnet Avenue. * **From Route 6:** At “the Octopus” intersection, turn north onto Pleasant Street, then turn right onto Hillman Street to take the overpass across Route 18. Turn left on Acushnet Avenue. * **From I-195 eastbound:** Exit at Penniman Street and turn right onto Purchase Street. Turn left at Logan Street to take the underpass, then turn right onto Acushnet Avenue. * **From I-195 westbound:** Take the exit for Downtown New Bedford, onto Route 18. Stay in the right lane and take the first exit for Weld Street. Turn left on Purchase Street. Turn left at Logan Street to take the underpass, then turn right onto Acushnet Avenue. **Church Street Station** is directly off Church Street near the intersection with Carlisle Street, and the routes there are much simpler: * **From neighborhoods east of Route 140:** Just head west until you reach Church Street.  * **From neighborhoods west of Route 140:** Use Kings Highway or Nash Road to get to Church Street. * **From Route 140 southbound:** Take Exit 5 onto Church Street. Or, take Exit 4 onto Mount Pleasant Street, then turn left onto Kings Highway, then right onto Park Avenue and another right onto Church Street. Parking [will be free](https://www.mass.gov/news/healey-driscoll-administration-mbta-announce-free-south-coast-rail-service-through-the-end-of-march) at South Coast stations through the end of April as part of a special promotion to encourage people to ride the train. Fares will also be free through the end of March and every weekend through the end of April,  After that, parking will be $4 a day on weekdays and $2 on weekends. You are allowed to leave your car overnight, MBTA officials said at a recent meeting. Find more policies on the [MBTA’s parking page](https://www.mbta.com/parking/parking-rules-and-policies). * * * ### [Local news needs your support before the year ends ⇢](https://newbedfordlight.org/support-our-publication/) * * * You can pay for parking at most MBTA lots using the [PayByPhone app](https://www.mbta.com/parking/pay-day), but not at the Whale’s Tooth parking lot at New Bedford Station. It will have its own text-to-pay system called XPressPark. The Whale’s Tooth lot, which used to serve only as Seastreak Ferry parking, is managed by the New Bedford Port Authority instead of the MBTA. The Port Authority released information on its separate parking system Monday night. The Whale’s Tooth lot’s daily rates will be the same as other MBTA lots, and it will participate in the free parking promotion in April. But anyone parking overnight will have to pay $15 per day. The lot will have 150 spaces reserved for train passengers and 570 for ferry passengers. ### **On public transportation** Fare-free [SRTA buses](https://www.srtabus.com/new-bedford/) have stops close to both train stations. [Route 202](https://www.srtabus.com/wp-content/uploads/202_FY25_Dec.pdf) toward Lund’s Corner and [Route 204](https://www.srtabus.com/wp-content/uploads/204_FY25_Dec.pdf) toward Ashley Boulevard run along Purchase Street — from there, riders can take the new pedestrian bridge across Route 18 to reach **New Bedford Station**. [Route 211](https://www.srtabus.com/wp-content/uploads/211_FY25_Dec.pdf) toward Fairhaven runs even closer to the station along Acushnet Avenue. SRTA buses don’t go directly past **Church Street Station**, but the [Route 221](https://www.srtabus.com/wp-content/uploads/221_FY25_Dec.pdf) North End shuttle stops at the Kings Highway Stop & Shop, a 15-minute walk from the station. The routes run as early as 5:20 a.m. and as late as 9:38 p.m., running about every half hour throughout the day. During early and late hours when the buses aren’t running but MBTA trains are, SRTA plans to add [“microtransit” vans](https://newbedfordlight.org/srta-rushing-to-prep-for-south-coast-rail/) that riders can call on an app, like an Uber. The microtransit service won’t be available in time for the South Coast Rail launch on March 24, because the MBTA moved the date up from the originally forecasted launch in May. But SRTA officials are rushing to launch the vans within the first few weeks of train service. _Email Grace Ferguson at gferguson@newbedfordlight.org_ _Editor’s note: This story was updated on ========================================================================================

The Herald News

Oct. 9, 2025, 4:05 a.m. ET

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=3230405883712927&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.heraldnews.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F10%2F09%2Fmbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026%2F86592754007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.heraldnews.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F10%2F09%2Fmbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026%2F86592754007%2F&text=Did%20MBTA%20underpay%20for%20Weaver%27s%20Cove%20in%20Fall%20River%3F%20Jury%20to%20decide%20eminent%20domain%20lawsuit&via=hnnow)[](mailto:?subject=Did%20MBTA%20underpay%20for%20Weaver's%20Cove%20in%20Fall%20River%3F%20Jury%20to%20decide%20eminent%20domain%20lawsuit%20-%20from%20Fall%20River%20Herald%20News&body=Did%20MBTA%20underpay%20for%20Weaver's%20Cove%20in%20Fall%20River%3F%20Jury%20to%20decide%20eminent%20domain%20lawsuit%0A%0AIn%20a%20land-taking%20lawsuit%20over%20South%20Coast%20Rail%2C%20the%20MBTA%20is%20being%20sued%20by%20the%20former%20owner%20of%20Weaver's%20Cove.%20A%20jury%20will%20hear%20the%20case.%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20heraldnews.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.heraldnews.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2025%2F10%2F09%2Fmbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026%2F86592754007%2F)

Keep Watching

*   The previous owner of Weaver's Cove said the MBTA took 68 acres of land by eminent domain but did not pay fair value.
*   The land is now the site of the Weaver's Cove layover station.
*   The MBTA has faced other eminent domain lawsuits regarding land-takings for South Coast Rail.

FALL RIVER — A jury next year will hear a lawsuit over the 2020 land-taking of [Weaver’s Cove](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2025/06/06/mbta-hears-south-coast-rail-complaints-over-noise-unreliability/84062523007/) where the MBTA has built [its commuter rail layover station](https://www.mass.gov/doc/weavers-cove-faq/download), another lawsuit for the MBTA in its series of land-takings to build South Coast Rail.

Weaver’s Cove Industrial Park LLC alleges it was not paid fair market value for 68 acres of land along North Main Street that [the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority](https://www.mbta.com/) took by eminent domain in February 2020.

In a 2022 civil lawsuit filed in Bristol County Superior Court, Weaver’s Cove Industrial Park LLC said it was “offered a sum of money as compensation for the taking of its land, which is grossly inadequate and does not reflect the fair market value.”

After years of court delays, on Monday, Oct. 6, attorneys for Weaver’s Cove and MBTA scheduled a jury trial to begin April 13, 2026.

![Image 2: MBTA commuter rail trains idle at 4:30 a.m. on May 7, 2025, at the Weaver's Cove Layover station in Fall River.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/)

The lawsuit does not disclose the amount the MBTA paid for the land.

Noise complaints: [Rumbling train noise at Fall River MBTA station is keeping neighbors awake all night](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/05/15/mbta-train-idling-keeps-neighbors-awake-in-fall-river-what-to-do/83626970007/)

What is on the Weaver's Cove layover site now?
----------------------------------------------

The site at 2680 N. Main St. is currently the site of the MBTA’s Weaver’s Cove Layover station; it contains a building for employees and a train yard where commuter trains on the Fall River/New Bedford Line are stored overnight and maintained.

The layover site has been subject to complaints from neighbors, who have said idling trains at the site [create excessive noise and vibrations overnight and in the early morning hours](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/05/15/mbta-train-idling-keeps-neighbors-awake-in-fall-river-what-to-do/83626970007/), disturbing sleep.

MBTA officials have said they are [exploring noise abatement options](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2025/07/10/mbta-south-coast-rail-schedule-changed-to-reduce-nighttime-noise/84538811007/).

![Image 3: The Weaver's Cove land is listed for sale in this 2016 file photo.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/)

What was on the Weaver's Cove land before?
------------------------------------------

The land was once the site of a Shell Oil terminal. Hess LNG and Weaver's Cove Energy bought the property in 2007 from construction magnate Jay Cashman for $16.8 million, with the goal of turning the site into a liquefied natural gas offloading facility.

A yearslong battle from environmental activists stopped the facility from being built, with plans abandoned in 2011.

![Image 4: Construction equipment sits on the site of the Weaver's Cove layover facility, part of the South Coast Rail project.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/)

The land sat vacant until Weaver’s Cove Industrial Park LLC, doing business as Thibeault Development, owned by William Thibeault, [purchased the property in February 2016 for $1.3 million](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/environment/2016/03/16/weaver-s-cove-energy-site/32385433007/).

Thibeault Development also owns the former Montaup power station across the Taunton River in Somerset.

'We want to regain your trust': [MBTA hears South Coast Rail reliability, noise complaints](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2025/06/06/mbta-hears-south-coast-rail-complaints-over-noise-unreliability/84062523007/)

![Image 5: Cars are parked at the Whale's Tooth parking lot at the New Bedford MBTA commuter rail station on Tuesday, April 1, 2025.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/)

Are there bathrooms on board? 10 common questions](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/12/mbta-commuter-rail-questions-dogs-tickets-bathrooms-food-and-more/82285343007/) [For students, seniors and low-income, rail has discounts. Who qualifies and how to apply.](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/02/19/mbta-commuter-south-coast-rail-reduced-fares-who-qualifies-and-how-to-apply/79114621007/) [SRTA to roll out MicroConnector: Book a ride to New Bedford, Fall River train stations](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/03/28/srta-microconnector-app-shuttle-service-south-coast-rail-stations-fall-river-new-bedford-ma/82708811007/) [Did MBTA underpay for Weaver's Cove in Fall River? Jury to decide eminent domain lawsuit](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/) [MBTA hears South Coast Rail reliability, noise complaints: 'We want to regain your trust'](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2025/06/06/mbta-hears-south-coast-rail-complaints-over-noise-unreliability/84062523007/) [These MBTA commuter rail schedule changes could reduce night-time noise, make trips faster](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/business/transportation/2025/07/10/mbta-south-coast-rail-schedule-changed-to-reduce-nighttime-noise/84538811007/)

![Image 6](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2025/10/09/mbta-eminent-domain-lawsuit-in-fall-river-scheduled-for-jury-in-2026/86592754007/)

Has the MBTA faced eminent domain claims before?
------------------------------------------------

In New Bedford, the MBTA took 8 acres of land to build its downtown passenger rail station, the Whale’s Tooth layover station and parking in five separate land-takings; it paid $486,627 for the land. The MBTA in July 2024 [reached a settlement with the city of New Bedford worth $3.5 million](https://www.heraldnews.com/story/news/2024/07/30/new-bedford-reaches-3-5-million-settlement-over-land-taken-by-mbta-eminent-domain/74599733007/).

In June 2019, the MBTA also took 180,000 square feet of land from BRK 1 LLC on Church Street in New Bedford to construct its Church Street station, paying $2.3 million for it. BRK 1 sued, claiming it was underpaid for the property. After a jury trial in August 2022 determined that the fair market value of the land was $3.5 million, the MBTA was ordered to pay BRK 1 an additional $1.2 million.

In Fall River, Tetreault Real Estate LLC owned about 36,000 square feet of land where the Fall River Depot station is currently located, at Davol and Pearce streets. The company sued in 2019 after the MBTA took the land by eminent domain, alleging it was compensated below fair market value at $226,400. The two parties settled for an undisclosed sum in 2022.

Updated Sept. 19, 2024, 12:24 p.m. ET

TAUNTON — “I’m confident everything we have now is on schedule,” MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng said at a South Coast Rail [presentation](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2024/09/11/mbta-manager-eng-plans-south-coast-rail-public-meeting-latest-updates/75165264007/) Wednesday evening at Taunton City Hall.

Eng said the plan the MBTA announced in June to have South Coast Rail operational by May 2025 is on track.

Construction is nearly complete on the $1 billion [South Coast Rail project](https://www.mbta.com/projects/south-coast-rail), which will connect passenger trains to Fall River, New Bedford and Taunton for the first time since 1958, linking the region to Boston. With the exception of a few components, all the train stations are either complete or have temporary certificates of occupancy.

![Image 1: MBTA General Manager Phillip Eng speaks at a South Coast Rail presentation in Taunton City Hall on Wednesday, Sept. 18, 2024.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2024/09/19/NTDG/75289205007-south-coast-rail-update-9182024-6.JPG?width=660&height=495&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Officials ride the rail ahead of meeting
----------------------------------------

Since this past summer, the trains, tracks, and signaling for cross walks have continued to undergo testing, with having the trains run the entire 37-mile length of South Coast Rail.

Before the presentation, a federally-authorized inspection ride occurred which carried members of the MBTA, along with numerous political officials, from the Middleboro station to New Bedford, at times reaching the rail’s top speed of 79 mph.  Eng said the trip lasted 29 minutes.

[State Rep. Bill Straus](https://malegislature.gov/Legislators/Profile/WMS1/Biography), a Mattapoisett Democrat who chairs House Joint Transportation Committee, was on the inspection ride.

Straus acknowledged the skepticism some in attendance felt regarding the pending completion of South Coast Rail.

“Everyone says ‘I’ll believe it when I see it.’  It takes on a reality when traveling in that train at high speeds.  It has been a long time coming,” Strauss said.

State Sen. Marc Pacheco, D-Taunton, was also on the inspection ride. He said while he “hoped a lot,” until he “pulled into those stations” he wondered if he would ever see South Coast Rail operational in his lifetime.

Said Pacheco: “This is a game-changer.”

![Image 2: From left, South Coast Rail Project Manager Jean Fox and Taunton Mayor Shaunna O'Connell attend an MBTA hosted presentation on South Coast Rail at Taunton City Hall on Wednesday, Sept. 18, 2024.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/09/19/south-coast-rail-commuter-train-taunton-mbta-station-fall-river-new-bedford/75289062007/)

90 days of test runs — minus passengers
---------------------------------------

South Coast Rail Executive Director Karen Antion said rigorous testing will continue for the remainder of the year. Then the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) will come in and, starting February 2025, conduct its own testing for 90 straight days.  During this 90-day “New Starts” period, the trains, stations, the signal crossings, dispatch, and staff will be operating daily like a regular commuter rail, without any customers on the train.

“Expect the trains to be running on the tracks at any time,” said Jean Fox, Project Manager for South Coast Rail, encouraging everyone to be aware and stay off the tracks.

The federal government has to certify the safety of all operations with South Coast Rail. Once the 90-day period is complete, and assuming success, the MBTA will be authorized to start serving the public.

Eng said every testing has variables, but “everything is going exactly as we have anticipated” and “we have every confidence we will get it done in that 90-day window.”

![Image 3: South Coast Rail Project Manager Jean Fox speaks at a presentation in Taunton City Hall on Wednesday, Sept. 18, 2024.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/09/19/south-coast-rail-commuter-train-taunton-mbta-station-fall-river-new-bedford/75289062007/)

The last delay
--------------

Back in spring, MBTA announced delays, once again, in the timeline of completion for South Coast Rail.

Eng explained his team realized the amount of testing that needed to be done, both on the state and federal levels, wasn’t going to meet the mid-2024 timetable given.

In addition, Eng brought up “materials” and “supply issues” regarding attaining final components for completing the East Taunton station.

State Sen. Mark Montigny, D-New Nedford, expressed his approval in MBTA committing to a date of operation.

“Establishing these firm commitments is paramount to building trust among our residents who have been subjected to too many false promises and unnecessary cheerleading over the years.  We look forward to the project’s final completion in May 2025,” Montigny said in a written statement.

Status of the East Taunton station
----------------------------------

South Coast Rail consists of six rail stations and two layover facilities. Though East Taunton has a certificate of occupancy, it isn’t complete yet.

South Coast Rail Chief Operating Officer Ryan Coholan said the East Taunton station is the most complex of the six stations due to features such as a center-island platform and an elevator.

Coholon said East Taunton has been the most challenging station to complete due to the contours of the land and overall topography.

Eng said presently it’s the elevator and access to the elevator that still need to be finished, and that has a timetable of the end of September/early October for completion.

Status of the New Bedford pedestrian bridge
-------------------------------------------

For the New Bedford station, [a new pedestrian bridge](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2023/06/13/pedestrian-bridge-work-underway-in-new-bedford-for-south-coast-rail/70307980007/) is being erected across Route 18 and Acushnet Avenue that will connect the station to the downtown area.

Presently, the bridge is 60% complete.

The steel arch structures are complete and visible.  What’s left are the elevator for the bridge and the sidewalks connected to each end of the bridge.

The bridge is scheduled to be complete in time for the opening of passenger service.

![Image 4: Former longtime Middleboro Selectman Frawley speaks during the Q&A portion of the South Coast Rail update in Taunton City Hall on Wednesday, Sept. 18, 2024.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/09/19/south-coast-rail-commuter-train-taunton-mbta-station-fall-river-new-bedford/75289062007/)

How many trips per weekday for Taunton, Fall River and New Bedford?
-------------------------------------------------------------------

According to Wednesday's presentation:

*   The New Bedford line will see 17 round trips to South Station in Boston during the average weekday.
*   The Fall River line will see 15 round trips to South Station during the weekday.
*   East Taunton will see 26 round trips during the weekday.

What about weekends and late at night?
--------------------------------------

In addition, the MBTA will offer 26 round trips over the weekend to South Station, across the whole South Coast Rail.

An official schedule isn’t complete yet. However, weekday direct service will run around every 70 minutes, while weekend direct service will run about every 120 minutes.

Late-night service will be offered for South Coast Rail, with the last train leaving Boston at just before midnight.

How much are tickets?
---------------------

The commuter rail is priced by zones, going from 1 to 10. All of South Coast Rail is Zone 8.

A Zone 8 fare to Boston is $12.25 each way. A reduced fare of $6 is available for people 65 or older, students and people with disabilities.

How much is parking?
--------------------

All South Coast Rail stations will have parking. This will include handicapped accessible parking and electric vehicle charging spots.

Parking will be $4 a day during weekdays and $2 a day on the weekends.

Is faster, cleaner Stoughton route ever going to happen?
--------------------------------------------------------

Eng said [Phase 2, known as the “Full Build,”](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2024/07/10/south-coast-rail-what-is-the-full-build-and-will-it-be-constructed/74346910007/) was not presently part of the [MBTA’s long-term Capital Investment Plan](https://www.mass.gov/news/massdot-board-approves-167-billion-five-year-capital-investment-plan), going all the way to fiscal year 2029.

Phase 2 would connect Taunton directly to Stoughton with additional stations built in Easton, Raynham and downtown Taunton, thereby bypassing the Middleboro/Lakeville commuter line. It is a shorter, more direct route, and would be faster and overall environmentally cleaner.

“Please tell me this is not a billion-dollar bait-and-switch,” exclaimed Allin Frawley, former longtime Middleboro Selectman and current member of the Planning Board, to the South Coast Rail team.

Frawley has been a vocal critic of the MBTA building a station in Middleboro over, among numerous things, the traffic, public safety, and environmental impacts it could have on his town.

He added, as an elected official, he had been told time and time again [over the years by MBTA officials](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/the-gazette/2019/05/10/selectmen-pick-up-south-coast/5199660007/) that the state was committed to completing Phase 2.

Project Manager Jean Fox explained the MBTA “has to focus on existing infrastructure that needs attention,” once South Coast Rail is operational.

She stated while Phase 2 isn’t part of the Capital Investment Plan, some funding remains to continue preliminary design work, for the possibility it can be done down the line.

60.content:
New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell declined to comment through a spokeswoman. A spokesman for the Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority on Friday defended taking the land, where the T is putting one of two new stations, parking spaces, and a train layover site.

“The MBTA appropriately exercised its eminent domain powers as provided by the Legislature and paid fair market value for all the properties taken,” spokesman Joe Pesaturo said.

The city’s lawsuit would be an unusual challenge of the T’s eminent domain authority, an area where litigation typically focuses on a property’s worth, attorneys and former state officials say. Even the consideration of a lawsuit surprised state lawmakers after New Bedford officials spent years advocating for the project alongside local business leaders and others.

Challenging the legality of the T’s seizures themselves would be an “interesting little twist,” said Peter Flynn, a veteran eminent domain attorney who last year represented a different New Bedford property owner whom a jury awarded $3.51 million, roughly $1.2 million more than what the MBTA originally paid that owner for other land it seized for the South Coast Rail project.

“If there is a challenge to the validity, it does put a pall of uncertainty over that project,” said Flynn, a former assistant attorney general. “If the MBTA proceeds on course and \[a judge determines\] they didn’t have the right to do what they’re doing, they’re doing that project at their peril.”

Jim Aloisi, a former state transportation secretary, called the draft complaint “pretty extraordinary.”

“This seems to be about money,” he said of the dispute. “But if you advocate and lobby for \[the rail connection\], the idea that you’d now be taking this action against the very entity you’ve been asking to do this . . . it’s biting the hand that fed you, in a way.”

![Image 1: New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell. "I’m a big supporter of the project," Mitchell said last year of South Coast Rail, "but I also think the public needs to be realistic about its benefits."](https://bostonglobe-prod.cdn.arcpublishing.com/resizer/v2/SWJJDWVOXJTLAP5CWNKHHSOWIY.jpg?auth=f90a39d44d4e16e01e3028a4104288f1f6bad2a337b5ee2914350de5020b3cbd&width=1440)

New Bedford Mayor Jon Mitchell. "I’m a big supporter of the project," Mitchell said last year of South Coast Rail, "but I also think the public needs to be realistic about its benefits."Jonathan Wiggs/Globe Staff

The South Coast Rail project, which would restore commuter rail service to the region for the first since the 1950s, has a tortured history, marked by stalled planning and [warnings](https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/2016/06/27/south-coast-rail-could-cost-billion-more-than-estimated/XxpSIfNX6FdNb7hnlz630L/story.html) about ballooning costs. But it gained traction in recent years after then-governor Charlie Baker’s administration embraced a plan to split the construction into phrases. In 2019, the state — not the MBTA — said it would pick up the [roughly $1 billion tab](https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/globelocal/2019/04/26/south-coast-rail-plan-reaches-milestone/n2X7zeXumReSsCEUhw1rcJ/story.html?p1=BGSearch_Overlay_Results&p1=Article_Inline_Text_Link) for the first phase of extending commuter rail service from Boston through Middleborough to New Bedford and Fall River.

The MBTA [said last year](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2022/12/05/metro/with-fall-river-extension-complete-south-coast-rail-is-track-open-late-2023-baker-mbta-announce/) that service is expected to start in late 2023, though officials have yet to set a formal date. It’s expected to take riders from Fall River and New Bedford about 90 minutes to reach Boston.

The T is constructing two stops in New Bedford for the project, one on Church Street and one near downtown, as well as a layover facility to store trains overnight.

But the city and the T are at odds over the value of the land the T seized. Portions of it were once part of the city’s “railroad depot project” site, which the city said it spent $17.3 million cleaning up, according to the complaint. After cobbling together insurance and other reimbursements, the net cost to the city was $9.9 million, the city said.

The MBTA’s offer amounted to a “fraction” of the city’s costs, according to the complaint.

The MBTA has used [eminent domain](https://www.wickedlocal.com/story/cohasset-mariner/2009/10/10/mbta-pays-1-875-for/39570458007/) for decades to [take land](https://www.seacoastonline.com/story/news/2003/05/03/mbta-says-it-will-take/51272993007/). The T and other public bodies can seize land as long as they show that it is in the public interest. They then must compensate the property owner for the land’s fair market value.

But New Bedford indicated it’s prepared to challenge more than the price. The city’s draft complaint, dated April 4 and crafted by lawyers from the Hingham firm Drohan Tocchio & Morgan, targets a series of land takings the T executed in 2020 and 2021. But in order for the T to build or expand any “mass transportation facilities,” the land itself had to already be “in the territory of the authority,” according to the complaint. At the time, the city was outside the MBTA’s service district; New Bedford residents [voted to formally join](https://newbedfordlight.org/new-bedford-voters-say-yes-to-south-coast-rail/) the MBTA in November 2022.

As a result, the city argued, the T “lacked authority to both provide for such construction, and to make the identified takings,” and the court should return the land to the city.

Even the potential for litigation set off alarm bells among the rail project’s supporters. **“**First off, I’m shocked,” said state Representative Chris Markey, a Democrat from nearby Dartmouth. “The act of actually drafting up a complaint means they’ve invested some time into it. I’m kind of perplexed.”

State Representative William Straus, a Mattapoisett Democrat who co-chairs the Legislature’s Transportation Committee, said the legal theory New Bedford is threatening “is a dangerous one” that could have a chilling effect on other MBTA expansion projects.

“If you’re threatening a lawsuit, it’s hard to see how that benefits New Bedford’s long-sought goal — and I’m talking 30, 40 years — to reconnect to the commuter rail,” he said. “I hope \[the T\] does not entertain this as a serious demand.”

Mitchell has vocally supported the project in the past, noting the city will not have to pay extra for the commuter rail to extend there. But he and others have also questioned how often residents will utilize it after the state opted for a slower route instead of building through the Hockomock Swamp, as initially considered.

In 2017, state officials projected the South Coast line could initially see 3,220 one-way trips — or about 1,600 riders taking a round trip. Yet, it’s unclear whether those pre-COVID-19 figures will hold as more people embrace remote work.

“I’m a big supporter of the project, but I also think the public needs to be realistic about its benefits,” Mitchell told [The Public’s Radio](https://thepublicsradio.org/article/in-bid-for-service-sooner-south-coast-rail-takes-the-long-way-to-boston) last year. “An indirect route to Boston on the rail is not going to usher in prosperity.”

Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board, said while he believes the T’s eminent domain powers extend statewide, “that’s never been tested.” He said he also was confident the project wouldn’t be derailed.

“The people of New Bedford, if you will, have spoken. It will happen,” he said. “It’s going to be a question of money, I guess.”

East Taunton (Now Running)
==========================

### [1141 County Street, Taunton, MA 02780](https://www.google.com/maps/place/1141+County+Street,+Taunton,+MA+02780)

East Taunton Station is a transfer and connection point to travel back and forth between Boston and the South Coast. Skip the traffic, reclaim your time, and take advantage of a relaxing commute to [South Station](https://massbytrain.com/stations/south-station/) for work, internships, or appointments by taking the train. It’s also a great option to get to your next concert, sporting event or other special events in the city.

Riders can transfer between connecting trains and direct trains at East Taunton station where the Fall River and New Bedford branches meet. This means riders on both branches can access more trips to or from South Station throughout the weekday.

We’ve coordinated train schedules to ensure that riders always have enough time to transfer at East Taunton.

Located right off Route 24, the East Taunton Station is a convenient location that provides plenty of parking and access to many destinations along the [Fall River/New Bedford Line](https://massbytrain.com/lines/fall-river-new-bedford/). Stop to explore attractions near [Quincy Center](https://massbytrain.com/stations/quincy-center/) and [JFK/UMass](https://massbytrain.com/stations/jfk-umass/), or take a quick trip south to [Fall River](https://massbytrain.com/stations/fall-river-depot/) or [New Bedford](https://massbytrain.com/stations/new-bedford/) and experience the amazing restaurants, museums and shops.

Updated March 3, 2025, 11:13 a.m. ET

*   The town of Middleboro, Massachusetts, is suing the state over a housing law that it claims it already complies with.
*   The town claims it has been unfairly penalized by the state for not complying with the law, including losing out on millions of dollars in grant funding.
*   Several other communities in Massachusetts have also pushed back against the MBTA Communities Act, arguing that it is too costly and burdensome.

MIDDLEBORO — “We believe we have the moral high ground to call out what’s unfair,” said Middleboro Select Board Chair Mark Germain at a press conference Friday afternoon.

He and other town official held the press conference to announce the town is suing the Commonwealth, Gov. Maura Healey, and the state’s Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities over forced compliance with a controversial multi-family housing law the town said it's already in compliance with.

Last fall, Middleboro Town Meeting [voted down a proposal](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/10/09/middleboro-ma-says-no-rejects-massachusetts-mbta-communities-act-multi-family-housing/75553660007/) to comply with the [MBTA Communities Act](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/mbta-communities-law-qa), a state mandate that requires all communities in the state with MBTA transit service establish a multi-acre overlay zoning district specifically for multi-family housing.

Every municipality with direct or adjacent transit service provided by the MBTA has to vote, or already has voted, on this mandate.

Town Manager James McGrail said the town already meets the law’s requirements for multi-family housing, but that the state won’t acknowledge its efforts.

He said the town is “taking a stand to defend the community” and to defend “our school district from arbitrary and draconian methods adopted by the Commonwealth to break communities.”

![Image 1: Middleboro Town Manager Jay McGrail speaks at a press conference on Friday, Feb. 28, 2025, at the Residences at Station Street announcing the town is suing the state over its multi-family housing law that requires communities with MBTA transit service create a multi-family housing zoning district. To the left are Select Board Chair Mark Germain and town attorney Gregg Corbo, center.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/02/28/NENT/80877050007-middlboro-presser-22825-mjc-1.jpg?width=660&height=656&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Here's what lawsuit is asking state to do
-----------------------------------------

Town attorney Gregg Corbo said he believes this will be a "landmark case." The town is seeking declaratory judgment and injunctive relief from the MBTA Communities Act, as well as prevention from the Commonwealth in enacting "arbitrary sanctions," said Corbo.

Middleboro officials say town is already in compliance
------------------------------------------------------

Middleboro's proposed district that was rejected at fall’s Town Meeting would have been on West Grove Street, within a half mile radius of the new MBTA station for South Coast Rail, located on South Main Street/Route 105, just off the I-495 exit ramps.

McGrail said the town already created a Smart Growth Zoning District that predates the state's multi-family housing law. According to a written statement from the town Friday, the district is comprised of 40.4 acres, all within a half-mile of an MBTA Commuter rail station and where multi-family housing is allowed of right at a density of 20 units per acre.

Within this district, McGrail said the town has built 881 housing units, with 250 of those units being affordable. He added there are numerous other housing developments the town has approved and are being built, such as a 108-unit complex, 27 of which will be affordable units, which will directly abut the new MSBA train station.

“Although the Town has clearly demonstrated that it is in compliance with the Act, it has been severely penalized because its choice of compliance methods is different than what a computer model says that an MBTA Community should look like,” the written statement from the town said.

![Image 2: Middleboro town attorney Gregg Corbo speaks at a press conference on Friday, Feb. 28, 2025, at the Residences at Station Street to announce the town is suing the state over its multi-family housing law that requires communities with MBTA transit service create a multi-family housing zoning district.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/02/28/NENT/80878806007-middlboro-presser-22825-mjc-3.jpg?width=660&height=591&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

Town manager: Middleboro is 'champion of affordable housing'
------------------------------------------------------------

McGrail said “the town is a champion of affordable housing." He said affordable/subsidizing housing represents 13.7% of the town's total housing stock, well above the minimum 10% requirement from the state.

The MBTA Communities Act specifically addresses multi-family housing, but not necessarily affordable housing.

Germain added while Middleboro has done everything it can to embrace smart growth that’s sustainable for the town and those in need of housing, “this law does nothing to address affordability in any form.”

![Image 3: Middleboro officials held a press conference on Friday, Feb. 28, 2025, at the at the Residences at Station Street, a housing development not far from the Middleboro train station, seen here, announcing the town is suing the state over its multi-family housing law that requires communities with MBTA transit service create a multi-family housing zoning district.](https://www.tauntongazette.com/gcdn/authoring/authoring-images/2025/02/28/NENT/80877052007-middlboro-presser-22825-mjc-2.jpg?width=660&height=439&fit=crop&format=pjpg&auto=webp)

State auditor calls multi-family housing law 'unfunded mandate'
---------------------------------------------------------------

A Feb. 21 letter from the state’s Division of Local Mandates and state Auditor Diana DiZoglio declared that the state's multi-family housing law is an “unfunded mandate.”

The written statement from Middleboro on Friday makes reference to that letter, saying "despite the Auditor’s determination, the state has made no effort to quantify the costs associated with complying with the Act, and the Attorney General has maligned the Auditor simply for doing her job.”

How would multi-family housing law cost town money?
---------------------------------------------------

Germain and other Middleboro officials have argued compliance with the mandate will increase housing production to an unsustainable level for the town. Middleboro officials previously said that it would result in a drastic increase in population — 18.5% over a few years – and that in turn would increase the cost of providing services such as schools, utilities, water and sewer infrastructure, and public safety.

“The state is not offering to pay for these upgrades,” said Germain.

Middleboro loses some state funding already
-------------------------------------------

The state’s Executive Office of Housing and Livable Communities [has told officials](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/09/30/middleboro-ma-multi-family-housing-district-zoning-massachusetts-mbta-communities-act/75374586007/) in municipalities that non-compliance with the multi-family housing law can result in legal action by the attorney general, as well as financial consequences, such as not being eligible for state grants.

Middleboro Town Planner Leann Bradley told officials at a September Planning Board meeting prior to the October Town Meeting that the town received close to $2 million in state grants over the last four years.

McGrail said at Friday's press conference the attorney general and governor have already committed “a gross misuse of power” by withholding several state grants previously approved for the town, including $73,000 for the Middleboro School District to launch and continue initiatives addressing mental health, as well as $2.8 million from MassWorks for infrastructural projects.

The written statement from the town also said, “State agencies, including the Department of Elementary and Secondary Education, informed Middleborough that it would no longer be receiving millions of dollars in state aid, which was promised to reimburse Middleborough for money it spent in reliance on those grants.”

Middleboro not alone in objections to state law
-----------------------------------------------

Numerous communities in the Commonwealth have refused to comply with the multi-family housing law.

In February 2024, the state attorney general’s office [sued Milton](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/04/01/milton-responds-to-states-mbta-communities-lawsuit/73140212007/) for rejecting the zoning requirement.

In September, [Middleboro selectmen voted unanimously](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/local/2024/09/30/middleboro-ma-multi-family-housing-district-zoning-massachusetts-mbta-communities-act/75374586007/) to submit an amicus brief supporting Milton in its legal battle with the attorney general.

In January of this year, [Massachusetts’ highest court ruled the multi-family housing law](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2025/01/08/milton-massachusetts-multifamily-housing-law-supreme-judical-court-ag-andrea-campbell/77518781007/) is indeed constitutional and enforceable by the Attorney General. However, the Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court also ruled that regulations passed to determine compliance did not go through the correct public process and were thus ineffective. This resulted in the state redoing the guidelines in order to make the law enforceable.

Recently, the Marshfield select board announced it [would seek a court order](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2025/02/28/mbta-communities-act-state-auditor-unfunded-mandate-marshfield-methuen-wrentham-middleboro-ma/80306543007/) to exempt it from compliance with the multi-family housing law until state funding is provided.

Marshfield voters previously [twice](https://www.tauntongazette.com/story/news/2024/04/23/marshfield-ma-town-meeting-mbta-zoning-transportation/73420298007/) rejected proposed zoning rules to comply with the state law at town meetings in 2024.
